scenario_stem:

Operations director Alice Brennan must strengthen control. She proposes electronic dashboards showing live waiting times in every branch, reviewed each Friday, at a cost of $31,000. Alternatively, branch managers could run weekly spot checks and phone in results, which is free but relies on self-reporting. Two branch managers privately admit they usually estimate rather than measure.

Reason 2: Controlling allows corrective action before problems grow [k]. Without monitoring, missed 20-minute targets would keep driving customers to rival pharmacies in the 2 towns [app].

scenario_stem:
Glenmore Dairy Co is a private limited company in Country X making fresh milk and yoghurt for 9 supermarket chains. General manager Ravi Menon leads 46 employees across pasteurising, packing and quality control, processing 18,500 litres of milk a day. Last year revenue reached $1.32 million. Ravi uses a democratic leadership style: a works council meets every Friday and staff ideas shaped last year's new yoghurt flavour, which lifted sales by 12%.

Glenmore has just won a contract requiring 22,000 litres a day from January, needing a new pasteuriser costing $85,000. The launch schedule allows only 6 weeks. Ravi is weighing a switch to autocratic leadership so he can impose decisions quickly, or keeping the democratic style workers are used to despite slower meetings.

Clear one-way instructions/close control of subordinates

Advantage 2: Employees who are consulted often feel valued, raising morale and motivation [k]; the Friday works council keeps 46 employees engaged in daily operations [app].

questions.model_answer: One reason for switching is speed: autocratic leadership means the leader decides alone and issues direct instructions [k]; the new contract requires 22,000 litres a day within 6 weeks and a pasteuriser costing $85,000, so fast unquestioned decisions could keep the launch on schedule [app], reducing the risk of late delivery penalties and protecting the $1.32 million revenue base [an]. scenario_stem:

Paula uses a democratic leadership style, holding a weekly 30-minute briefing where employees raise ideas; staff redesigned the breakfast menu this year, raising sales by 9%.

The events manager has resigned and Paula must choose a replacement. Marco, a reception supervisor, would continue her democratic style with the 6-person events team. scenario_stem:
Seaward Printworks is a private limited company in Country X producing marketing brochures, packaging and catalogues for 25 business customers. It is led by production director Omar Haddad, who manages 22 printers and finishers. Output last year was 940,000 printed items, with revenue of $1.28 million and unit costs of $0.86.

Omar has always kept close control of daily schedules. He now employs 5 senior designers who are highly skilled and self-motivated, and they complain that his daily checks slow them down. scenario_stem:
Northlight Software Ltd is a Country X technology company employing 43 staff, of whom 19 work from home in 5 different countries. The company builds booking software used by 11 hospitals, so deadlines matter. Teams coordinate through email and a weekly video meeting; everything else goes through a shared chat channel. Software builds are tracked on a spreadsheet updated by one senior developer.

Last quarter 14 project deadlines slipped and client complaints reached 31, which staff blame on slow, unclear email chains. The operations director proposes a project management platform costing $1,150 per month with task boards, deadlines and file sharing. The technical lead warns of 'message overload' and says weekly video contact should not be reduced. The platform would take 3 weeks to set up with 2 training sessions.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'electronic communication'.

knowledge_max_2: Communication using electronic devices and digital technology
Examples include email, video calls, chat apps and intranets

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of electronic communication for Northlight Software.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: It allows instant communication across long distances [k], so the 19 staff working from home in 5 different countries can message colleagues in seconds [app]. Advantage 2: It creates shareable written records [k], so task boards and shared files would replace the single spreadsheet now updated by one senior developer [app].

knowledge_max_2: Instant, low-cost communication across long distances
Creates permanent, shareable records of messages and files
application_max_2: 19 staff work from home in 5 different countries
Shared task boards would replace the spreadsheet updated by one senior developer

questions.question_text: Explain two problems with relying on email chains for coordination.

Problem 2: Email is slow for urgent decisions [k], so the 19 staff working from home across 5 different countries must wait hours for replies instead of seeing tasks and deadlines on a shared board [app], reducing productivity and morale [an].

knowledge_max_2: Long email chains are unclear and create barriers to understanding
Email is slow for urgent decisions compared with live tools
application_max_2: 14 project deadlines slipped and client complaints reached 31 last quarter
19 remote staff across 5 different countries wait on email replies rather than a shared board
analysis_max_2: Delayed, unclear work hurts the 11 hospitals waiting on the software

questions.question_text: Do you think the operations director should adopt the project management platform? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for the platform is that it costs $1,150 per month [k] but gives every team member the same live task boards, deadlines and shared files, replacing slow unclear email chains blamed for 14 slipped deadlines and 31 client complaints [app], so coordination would become faster and more transparent [an]. However, one argument against is that staff already suffer 'message overload' [k], and the platform would add another channel on top of the shared chat and email rather than removing them [app], which could reduce attention and cut the personal contact of the weekly video meeting [an]. Overall, Northlight should adopt the platform but make it the single source of task truth and keep the weekly video meeting [eval], because the platform's transparency outweighs its $1,150 monthly cost if it replaces rather than adds to email [eval].

scenario_stem:
Kestrelmoor Textiles Ltd runs a garment factory in Country X employing 150 machinists on day and night shifts. About 62 of the machinists are recent migrants whose first language is not English. Safety and quality instructions are issued as written English notices, and only 71% of migrant machinists passed last quarter's safety quiz, compared with 94% of other staff.

The factory manager must overcome this language barrier. Option one is to translate all safety and quality notices into 3 languages at a cost of $7,200. Option two is to pay 6 bilingual supervisors an extra $180 per month each to give verbal demonstrations on the line, costing $1,080 a month. Both options aim to cut the 9 safety incidents recorded last year.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'communication barrier'.
questions.model_answer: A communication barrier is anything that stops a message being received or understood correctly, such as language differences, noise, jargon, poor timing or unclear wording. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Anything that blocks or distorts a message between sender and receiver
Examples include language, noise, jargon and unclear wording

questions.question_text: Explain two barriers to communication at Kestrelmoor Textiles.
questions.model_answer: Barrier 1: Language differences [k], 62 of the 150 machinists are recent migrants whose first language is not English, so written English notices are not fully understood [app]. Barrier 2: Over-reliance on written English notices [k], only 71% of migrant machinists passed last quarter's safety quiz compared with 94% of other staff [app].

knowledge_max_2: Language difference blocks understanding of messages
Using an unsuitable method (written-only) blocks understanding
application_max_2: 62 of the 150 machinists are recent migrants whose first language is not English
Only 71% of migrant machinists passed the safety quiz versus 94% of other staff

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of option one, translating the notices into 3 languages.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: All migrant machinists receive instructions in their own language [k], so the 62 recent migrants would understand written safety and quality notices without depending on a supervisor being present [app], reducing the gap between the 71% and 94% pass rates [an]. Advantage 2: Translation is a one-off cost with no ongoing fees [k], at $7,200 once compared with $1,080 every month for bilingual supervisors [app], saving money after about 7 months and keeping instructions available at all times [an].

knowledge_max_2: Instructions in the reader's own language remove the language barrier
A one-off translation has no recurring monthly cost
application_max_2: 62 recent migrants would understand notices without a supervisor present
$7,200 once versus $1,080 a month for bilingual supervisors
analysis_max_2: Pass rates should rise towards the 94% benchmark of other staff
Translation is cheaper after about 7 months and always available

questions.question_text: Do you think the factory manager should translate the notices instead of paying bilingual supervisors? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for translating the notices is the one-off cost of $7,200 [k], which would give all 62 recent migrants written instructions in 3 languages, cheaper than $1,080 a month for supervisors after about 7 months [app], reducing the language barrier that left only 71% passing the safety quiz [an]. However, one argument against is that written notices cannot demonstrate tasks [k], so machinists who struggle to read in any language would still fail, while verbal demonstrations by 6 bilingual supervisors would show safe machine operation directly on the line [app], which better suits practical garment work and immediate questions [an]. Overall, the manager should choose option two, the bilingual supervisors [eval], because hands-on demonstration overcomes the language barrier more reliably in a factory, and it can be scaled back once pass rates reach 94% and the 9 safety incidents fall [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Translated written instructions remove the language barrier permanently
Verbal demonstration teaches practical tasks and allows questions
application_max_2: $7,200 once for 3 languages versus $1,080 a month for 6 bilingual supervisors
Only 71% of migrant machinists passed the safety quiz versus 94% of others
analysis_max_2: Permanent translated notices close the comprehension gap at low cost
Written-only methods cannot teach physical machine operation
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both the translation and the bilingual supervisor options
Reaches a justified recommendation using stem figures

scenario_stem:
Brackmore Insurance Services runs a customer call centre in Country X with 88 call-handlers answering about 30,000 calls a month. Call quality is monitored by a small team of 4 quality coaches. Complaints are logged by handlers, and a weekly email tells all staff the top 5 complaint types. Handlers receive no individual feedback and never hear what happened to complaints they logged.

Only 12% of staff in last year's survey felt their feedback was acted on. The centre manager proposes monthly one-to-one feedback meetings between team leaders and handlers, using about 140 staff-hours a month. Team leaders instead suggest a daily 10-minute briefing with the whole team, which would take no extra time beyond shift handovers. Waiting times already average 9 minutes, so staff motivation matters.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'feedback'.
questions.model_answer: Feedback is the response sent back to the sender of a message, showing whether it was received and understood, or giving a reaction to a performance, idea or action. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Response returned to the sender of a message
Shows whether the message was understood or comments on performance

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why feedback is important for Brackmore call-handlers.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Feedback tells handlers whether their work meets standard [k], so the 88 call-handlers would know how they performed on the about 30,000 calls a month [app]. Reason 2: Feedback motivates employees and helps them improve [k], which matters because only 12% of staff felt their feedback was acted on last year [app].

knowledge_max_2: Feedback tells employees whether their work meets the standard
Feedback motivates employees and supports improvement
application_max_2: 88 call-handlers answer about 30,000 calls a month
Only 12% of staff felt their feedback was acted on last year

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of relying only on the weekly email of complaint types.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The email is one-way and gives no personal comment [k], so the 88 handlers cannot learn how their own handling of the about 30,000 calls a month could improve [app], limiting learning and call quality [an]. Problem 2: Emails list only the top 5 complaint types [k], so unusual or individual issues raised by handlers are never acknowledged, consistent with only 12% feeling their feedback was acted on [app], leaving staff feeling ignored and demotivated [an].

knowledge_max_2: One-way channels give no personal, tailored guidance
Summaries hide individual and unusual issues
application_max_2: 88 handlers answer 30,000 calls a month with no individual feedback
The weekly email lists only the top 5 complaint types and 12% felt heard
analysis_max_2: Without tailored guidance, call quality and learning stagnate
Ignored handlers become demotivated and waiting times may rise

questions.question_text: Do you think the centre manager should introduce monthly one-to-one feedback meetings instead of daily team briefings? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for one-to-one meetings is that handlers receive personal feedback [k], using about 140 staff-hours a month to discuss individual performance, which would address the finding that only 12% of staff felt their feedback was acted on [app], so handlers would know exactly how to improve their handling of the about 30,000 calls a month [an]. However, one argument against is the time cost [k], as 140 staff-hours a month is the equivalent of about 18 working days, and a daily 10-minute briefing with the whole team would cost no extra time beyond shift handovers [app], reaching all 88 handlers daily instead of once a month [an]. Overall, the centre should combine both, starting with the daily briefings and adding monthly one-to-one meetings for struggling handlers [eval], because briefings cost nothing extra while one-to-ones fix the deeper motivation problem behind the 12% figure [eval].

knowledge_max_2: One-to-one feedback is personal but time-consuming
Group briefings are broad, cheap and can be frequent
application_max_2: 140 staff-hours a month is about 18 working days of one-to-one time
Only 12% of staff felt their feedback was acted on last year
analysis_max_2: Personal feedback addresses individual performance on 30,000 calls
Daily briefings cost nothing extra and reach everyone far more often
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both the one-to-one meetings and daily briefings
Reaches a justified recommendation using stem figures

scenario_stem:
Ruskin & Cole Department Store in Country X employs 210 people across 2 selling floors and a warehouse. The store turns over $24 million in sales a year. Head office communicates every change, till updates, floor moves and rota rules, by email and memo, and full staff meetings are held only twice a year. A staff survey found 58% of employees did not understand the last 3 changes, and staff turnover rose to 34% this year.

Regional manager Dana Cole proposes fortnightly 45-minute team briefings where staff can ask questions; the finance director prefers a quarterly newsletter costing $300 per edition, about $1,200 a year. Dana argues face-to-face questions would catch confusion early, but the finance director notes the briefings would use about 158 staff-hours each fortnight across all 210 employees. The newsletter would reach all 210 employees.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'two-way communication'.
questions.model_answer: Two-way communication is communication where the receiver can respond to the sender, such as a conversation, meeting or phone call, allowing questions and feedback. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Message flows in both directions with feedback
Allows questions and clarification, unlike one-way channels

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of two-way communication at the store.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Staff can ask questions and clear up confusion immediately [k], so the 58% of employees who did not understand the last 3 changes could be brought up to date in fortnightly briefings [app]. Benefit 2: Managers learn what employees think [k], helping the store reduce the staff turnover that rose to 34% this year by showing staff their views matter [app].

knowledge_max_2: Two-way channels allow questions and immediate clarification
Two-way channels make staff feel heard and valued
application_max_2: 58% of employees did not understand the last 3 changes
Staff turnover rose to 34% this year

questions.question_text: Explain two problems caused by one-way email and memo communication at Ruskin & Cole.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: One-way messages cannot be questioned [k], so the 58% of staff who misunderstood recent till updates and rota rules had no chance to ask about them between staff meetings held only twice a year [app], causing mistakes and frustration on the shop floor [an]. Problem 2: One-way communication makes staff feel unheard [k], which may explain why staff turnover rose to 34% this year, with employees leaving rather than raising concerns by email to head office [app], increasing recruitment and training costs [an].

knowledge_max_2: One-way messages cannot be questioned or clarified
One-way communication leaves staff feeling ignored
application_max_2: 58% of staff misunderstood recent changes, meetings held only twice a year
Staff turnover rose to 34% this year amid email and memo communication
analysis_max_2: Unquestioned instructions cause mistakes and frustration on the shop floor
Feeling unheard drives staff turnover and raises recruitment costs

questions.question_text: Do you think Ruskin & Cole should introduce fortnightly team briefings instead of a quarterly newsletter? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for the briefings is that they are two-way [k], letting the 210 staff ask questions about till updates and rota rules, attacking the 58% misunderstanding directly, at a cost of about 158 staff-hours each fortnight [app], which should reduce errors, the 34% staff turnover and disruption to the $24 million sales [an]. However, one argument against is cost and reach [k], as 158 staff-hours every fortnight is far more expensive in time than a $300 quarterly newsletter costing about $1,200 a year, which reaches everyone in print [app], but the newsletter is one-way and would not fix the misunderstanding driving the 34% turnover [an]. Overall, the store should introduce the fortnightly team briefings [eval], because two-way face-to-face communication addresses the root cause, and falling turnover would save far more than the briefings cost [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Two-way face-to-face briefings check understanding
A printed newsletter is cheap and reaches everyone but is one-way
application_max_2: 158 staff-hours each fortnight to answer the 58% misunderstanding
$300 per edition, about $1,200 a year for the newsletter
analysis_max_2: Two-way dialogue reduces errors, turnover of 34% and disruption to $24 million sales
The one-way newsletter would not fix the misunderstanding causing turnover
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both the fortnightly briefings and the quarterly newsletter
Reaches a justified recommendation using stem figures

scenario_stem:
Castlereagh Solicitors is a law firm in Country X with 52 staff across 3 offices. The partners plan to merge with a rival firm, Trelawney & Grant, moving 30 staff into new premises 12 miles away and creating 12 new roles. No announcement has been made; rumours have spread through the grapevine and 7 staff have resigned in 2 months.

The managing partner must decide how to announce the merger. Option one is an all-staff meeting followed by written letters to every employee. Option two is to issue a press release this week first; the partners believe it would reassure clients of continuity, but staff would hear of the merger from the media. The deal is worth $2.4 million to the firm.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'formal communication'.
questions.model_answer: Formal communication is communication sent through the official, authorised channels and methods of an organisation, such as official letters, memos, meetings and press releases issued by managers. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Communication via the official, authorised channels of the organisation
Examples include official letters, meetings, memos and press releases

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of formal communication for Castlereagh Solicitors.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Formal channels carry authority and accuracy [k], so an all-staff meeting followed by letters would tell all 52 staff the official merger details rather than grapevine rumours [app]. Advantage 2: Formal written records can be referred back to [k], so the 30 staff moving to premises 12 miles away would have clear written terms about their relocation and the 12 new roles [app].

knowledge_max_2: Official channels are accurate and carry authority
Written formal records can be referred back to
application_max_2: All 52 staff would hear official details instead of rumours
30 staff moving 12 miles away would have written terms on the 12 new roles

questions.question_text: Explain two problems caused by rumours and informal communication about the merger.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Rumours are inaccurate and uncontrolled [k], so staff imagine job losses across the 3 offices even though the plan creates 12 new roles and relocates 30 staff rather than cutting jobs [app], fuelling anxiety and resignations [an]. Problem 2: Informal communication undermines trust in management [k], which is why 7 staff resigned in 2 months without any official announcement being made [app], risking client service and jeopardising the $2.4 million deal [an].

knowledge_max_2: Rumours are inaccurate and cannot be controlled by the business
Silence from management damages trust and morale
application_max_2: Rumours ignore the 12 new roles and 30 staff relocation across 3 offices
7 staff resigned in 2 months before any official announcement
analysis_max_2: Imagined job losses fuel anxiety and resignations
Resignations risk client service and the $2.4 million deal

questions.question_text: Do you think Castlereagh should tell staff first through an all-staff meeting and letters rather than issuing a press release this week? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for telling staff first is that it is honest and builds trust [k], so the 52 staff would hear directly from the managing partner before a press release, preventing more resignations like the 7 staff who left in 2 months [app], protecting morale and client service during the $2.4 million merger [an]. However, one argument against is that a press release this week would reassure clients and protect the firm's reputation sooner [k], because rival firms may already know about the merger talks [app], yet staff hearing first from the media would feel betrayed and may leave before the 12 new roles are filled [an]. Overall, the firm should hold the all-staff meeting and written letters first, then issue the press release [eval], because committed staff are essential during a merger and a one-week delay for clients is a small price compared with losing key lawyers [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Telling staff first builds trust and commitment
Early public announcement reassures clients and protects reputation
application_max_2: 52 staff would hear directly, stopping the 7 resignations seen in 2 months
Press release first would reach clients sooner but staff would feel betrayed
analysis_max_2: Honesty protects morale, client service and the $2.4 million deal
Media-first news risks losing staff before the 12 new roles are filled
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both announcing to staff first and issuing a press release first
Reaches a justified recommendation using stem figures

scenario_stem:
Wrenhill Toys Ltd sells the wooden 'Sunshine Express' train set through 160 retailers across Country X; about 9,000 units were sold last year. The train set sells for $45 and is the firm's best-selling toy this Christmas. A small number of units contain loose magnets, a choking risk identified by the safety regulator, and 340 sets have already been returned by parents.

The marketing manager proposes an urgent press release and social media campaign to alert buyers quickly. The managing director prefers phoning all 160 retailers and writing to the 2,100 buyers who registered online, costing about $6,500 and taking 2 weeks; only retailers and the media can reach the remaining 6,900 unregistered buyers. The managing director worries a public campaign would alarm parents who never bought the set.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'written communication'.
questions.model_answer: Written communication is the passing of information through written words, such as letters, emails, memos, reports, notices or text messages, producing a record that can be read and re-read. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Communication using written words
Examples include letters, emails, reports and notices; creates a record

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of written communication for the product recall.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Written messages give a permanent record [k], so the 160 retailers would have the recall instructions in writing to identify and return the unsafe Sunshine Express sets [app]. Advantage 2: Written communication suits messages sent to named individuals [k], so the 2,100 buyers who registered online would receive clear return instructions by letter [app].

knowledge_max_2: Written messages create a permanent, checkable record
Written messages suit sending the same message to named individuals
application_max_2: 160 retailers would have recall instructions in writing for the unsafe sets
2,100 registered online buyers would receive return instructions by letter

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of announcing the recall through a press release and social media.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Mass electronic channels reach far more people far faster [k], alerting the 6,900 unregistered buyers who never registered online [app], so unsafe Sunshine Express sets can be returned before more magnets are swallowed [an]. Advantage 2: Posting online costs almost nothing [k], compared with about $6,500 and 2 weeks for phone calls and letters to retailers and registered buyers [app], protecting public safety and the brand at minimal cost [an].

knowledge_max_2: Mass media and social media reach huge audiences quickly
Electronic public announcements cost very little
application_max_2: 6,900 unregistered buyers would be reached instantly
Compared with about $6,500 and 2 weeks for phone calls and letters
analysis_max_2: Faster alerts return unsafe sets before more injuries occur
Minimal cost protects both public safety and the brand's reputation

questions.question_text: Do you think Wrenhill Toys should rely on the press release and social media instead of phoning retailers and writing to registered buyers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: One argument for the press release and social media is speed and reach [k], which would instantly alert the owners of the remaining 6,900 unregistered units, including the 340 sets already proving defective [app], so children could be protected immediately at almost no cost [an]. However, one argument against is that mass media cannot guarantee every affected buyer acts [k], whereas phoning the 160 retailers and writing to the 2,100 registered buyers uses two-way and written channels with confirmed receipt, costing about $6,500 and 2 weeks [app], giving an auditable recall record for the safety regulator [an]. Overall, Wrenhill should use both: the press release immediately to protect children, followed by calls and letters to retailers and registered buyers to evidence the recall [eval], prioritising safety over the $6,500 cost [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Mass media is fast and wide-reaching but unverifiable
Two-way and written channels confirm receipt and create records
application_max_2: Press coverage reaches the 6,900 unregistered buyers instantly
Phoning 160 retailers and writing to 2,100 registered buyers costs about $6,500
analysis_max_2: Immediate public alert prevents further injuries from loose magnets
Confirmed calls and letters give an auditable record for the regulator
evaluation_max_2: Weighs both the public campaign and direct two-way contact
Reaches a justified recommendation using stem figures

scenario_stem:

scenario_stem:

The inspection team requires graduates who can read technical drawings, operate measurement equipment and write safety reports. Benefit 2: It links appointees to the real demands of the job [k], so graduates appointed to the inspection team can handle technical drawings, measurement equipment and safety reports [app], reducing costly mistakes across 14 active bridge contracts [an].

scenario_stem:
Brackmere City Council employs 1,150 staff delivering waste collection, leisure centres and social care in Country X. The council uses a standard application form for all vacancies and received 260 applications for 8 administrative officer posts last year. Councillors have asked whether the council should accept CVs instead, arguing the form is outdated and discourages younger applicants from applying.

The form guarantees every candidate supplies the same information, supporting fair, consistent shortlisting and the council's equal opportunities policy. Moving to CVs could modernise recruitment, but officers estimate rewriting the process would cost $4,500 and take 3 months, and 90% of councils in comparable regions still use application forms for consistency and legal defensibility. The form is also translated into 2 community languages.

scenario_stem:
Foxbury Flour Mills is a private limited company in Country X, founded 9 years ago by siblings Dana and Cole Foxbury. It mills wheat into flour for 60 bakeries across the region, employing 24 millers and drivers, and last year milled 9,000 tonnes of flour. The company uses cost-plus pricing, applying a 25% markup to a production cost that has risen from $0.80 per kilogram to $0.88 and now $0.96.

The cost-plus price has therefore moved from $1.00 to $1.10 per kilogram. Keeping the 25% markup would lift the price to $1.20. Rival Harborpoint Flour sells at $1.15 per kilogram, and two large bakeries warned they will switch suppliers if prices rise again. Cole wants to hold at $1.10 and absorb the extra cost, while Dana wants the full increase passed on. The directors must decide within one month.

questions.question_text: Define 'cost-plus pricing'.

It is also straightforward to calculate and easy to update as costs change [k], as shown by the price moving from $1.00 to $1.10 per kilogram and possibly to $1.20 [app].

scenario_stem:
Harborview Electrical is a private limited company in Country X, founded 6 years ago by owner Priya Nair. It sells televisions, refrigerators and small appliances from two high-street shops, employing 16 staff including delivery drivers. Last year it sold 2,400 televisions at an average price of $599 against a unit cost of $410, generating $1.44 million in revenue and a profit of $0.30 million.

National chain ValueMart has cut its television prices to $549 and runs match-any-price weekend promotions. Priya can either hold $599 and rely on free delivery and expert advice, or lower to $549 to match ValueMart. Matching cuts Harborview's profit margin per television from $189 to $139, and she fears sales could fall by 20% if the higher price is held. She must set the television price for the key summer trading period.

questions.question_text: Define 'competitive pricing'.

It also helps prevent losing customers to cheaper competitors [k], protecting Harborview's 2,400 television sales and $1.44 million annual revenue [app].

Competitive pricing also makes Harborview dependent on rivals' decisions [k], so ValueMart's match-any-price weekends may force repeated price cuts [app], eroding margins in the two shops without any guarantee of extra volume [an].

It offers a gym, pool and studio classes with capacity for 1,500 members and employs 22 full-time trainers and reception staff. Rival Capital Fitness charges $45 per month, has 900 members, and Turnbridge has spent $80,000 on launch advertising so far.

To attract members quickly, Marcus is considering penetration pricing: $25 per month for the first 3 months, after which membership rises to $42 per month. Each machine is delivered within 8 weeks of order and includes a 2-year parts warranty. Currently sales are handled by an agent who earns a 6% commission and knows the bakery trade well. Alternatively, Rusthaven could employ a full-time technical sales representative at $55,000 a year to visit and demonstrate machines to around 90 bakery owners. The representative would keep the full margin, but the salary would be paid whatever the sales result.

questions.question_text: Define 'place' in the marketing mix.
questions.model_answer: In the marketing mix, place refers to where and how goods and services are made available to customers, that is the channels of distribution used to reach them [2].

knowledge_max_2: refers to where and how products/services are made available to customers
concerns the channels of distribution used to reach the customer

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Rusthaven Engineering Ltd of using an agent to sell its bakery machines.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: The agent already knows the bakery trade and its buyers [k], so Rusthaven gains immediate access to bakery owners it might never reach alone [app]. Benefit 2: The agent is paid only a 6% commission on machines actually sold [k], so Rusthaven carries no fixed salary cost and avoids the risk of paying $55,000 a year before any sales are made [app].

knowledge_max_2: an agent brings local or trade market knowledge and buyer relationships
an agent is paid commission only, so there is no fixed cost before sales are made
application_max_2: access to bakery owners through the agent's trade knowledge
6% commission only, avoiding a guaranteed $55,000 a year salary

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Rusthaven Engineering Ltd of employing its own technical sales representative rather than an agent.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A technical representative would demonstrate machines to around 90 bakery owners, giving live technical walkthroughs and trials [k], which is ideal for a $28,000 machine that bakeries want to see working before buying [app], raising the conversion of demonstrations into sales [an]. Benefit 2: The representative works exclusively for Rusthaven [k], so pricing, messaging and service are fully controlled by Rusthaven rather than by an outside agent acting for its own commission [app], protecting margins and brand image on every $28,000 sale [an].

knowledge_max_2: a technical representative can demonstrate complex products directly to buyers
an exclusive representative gives the firm control over pricing and messaging
application_max_2: live demonstrations to around 90 bakery owners for a $28,000 machine
Rusthaven keeps control of every $28,000 sale instead of relying on a commission-driven agent
analysis_max_2: technical demonstrations build buyer confidence and lift conversion rates
full control over the sales process protects margins and brand consistency

questions.question_text: Do you think Rusthaven Engineering Ltd should replace the agent with its own sales representative? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Replacing the agent with a representative at $55,000 a year would cost less than the 6% commission last year, about $75,600 on $1,260,000 of revenue [k], saving around $20,600 a year before counting extra sales from 90 bakery-owner demonstrations [app]. A dedicated representative could build direct relationships, feed back market information and sell the full range of machines with live technical support [an]. However, the $55,000 salary is a fixed cost paid even in a weak year, when the agent would have cost nothing, and the agent's trade contacts and motivation to close deals could be lost [k]; commission may push an agent to sell more aggressively than a salaried employee [app], so revenue could fall below $1,260,000 during the transition [an]. Overall, Rusthaven should replace the agent, because $75,600 of commission exceeds the $55,000 salary and direct control suits high-value technical machines [eval], but it should set clear sales targets and keep the agent on a handover period of a few months to protect customer relationships [eval].

knowledge_max_2: a fixed salary can cost less than percentage commission on current revenue
however, a salary is paid regardless of sales, unlike commission, and incumbent trade contacts are lost
application_max_2: 6% commission on $1,260,000 is about $75,600 a year versus $55,000 for a representative
saving about $20,600 a year, plus upside from demonstrations to 90 bakery owners
analysis_max_2: dedicated representative builds direct relationships and gathers market intelligence
transition risk: fixed cost, lost agent motivation and possible revenue dip below $1,260,000
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation favouring replacement given the commission saving and control benefits
balanced judgement recommending targets and a short handover period to manage risk

scenario_stem:
Rowanhill Knitwear is a private limited company designing and knitting wool sweaters and cardigans in Country X. Founded 8 years ago, it employs 40 staff and sells through 80 independent clothes shops and 2 department stores. Revenue last year was $2.4 million.

Half of revenue comes from sweaters and cardigans sold in autumn and winter, so stock must be ready by September. The directors must choose a route to grow sales. They could launch their own online shop at a cost of $40,000, with packaging and postage adding about $6 per garment, or they could sign a deal with Haversham Wholesale, which would place Rowanhill Knitwear in 120 shops but demand a 20% discount on trade prices. Online trials suggest 5% of parcels would come back as returns, and customers cannot try garments before buying.

Problem 2: Knitwear is seasonal and visual, so Rowanhill must keep improving photography and website content to compete online [k], adding ongoing spending beyond the $6 per garment packaging and postage [app].

Benefit 2: Haversham manages ordering, warehousing and delivery to shops [k], taking over logistics so Rowanhill's 40 staff can focus on design and knitting [app], lowering strain on the business while the 2 department store relationships continue [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Rowanhill Knitwear should sign with Haversham Wholesale rather than launch its own online shop? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Signing with Haversham Wholesale would instantly widen distribution from 80 to 120 shops, so sales could rise well beyond $2.4 million without the $40,000 website build or the 5% return headache [k]. Overall, Rowanhill should sign with Haversham now, because immediate volume into 120 shops beats waiting for online traction [eval], but it should renegotiate the 20% discount after 12 months of results and start building its online presence once cash flow improves [eval].

scenario_stem:
Saltpan Lobster Co is a family fishing business in Country X, founded 7 years ago, employing 8 fishermen on 2 boats. It lands about 30 tonnes of live lobsters a year. Around 80% are sold to a wholesale fish market at $14 per kg and 20% go directly to 12 local restaurants at $22 per kg. Revenue last year was $468,000.

The owners could spend $25,000 on a refrigerated van to deliver live lobsters to 20 more restaurants each week. The 2 boats fish 5 days a week, weather permitting, and landings peak in July and August. However, lobsters sold wholesale need no marketing or extra staff, payments arrive reliably, and the wholesale market currently takes every lobster the boats land.

questions.question_text: Define 'intermediary'.
questions.model_answer: An independent business that helps move goods from producer to consumer, for example wholesalers, retailers or agents, earning a margin or commission for its role [2].

knowledge_max_2: an independent business between producer and consumer
includes wholesalers, retailers or agents, earning a margin or commission

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why selling lobsters directly to restaurants suits a perishable product such as live lobsters.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Live lobsters are perishable, so every hour of transit matters [k], meaning short direct trips to the 12 local restaurants keep them fresher than a longer journey through the wholesale fish market [app]. Reason 2: Selling direct removes intermediary handling and margins [k], so Saltpan can charge $22 per kg instead of $14 per kg, keeping an extra $8 per kg on every lobster sold direct [app].

knowledge_max_2: perishable goods need the shortest possible channel to stay fresh
selling direct avoids the intermediary's margin or mark-up
application_max_2: short direct trips to 12 local restaurants keep lobsters fresher than the wholesale route
$22 per kg direct versus $14 per kg wholesale, an extra $8 per kg

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why wholesale markets remain important to fishing businesses such as Saltpan Lobster Co.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The wholesale fish market takes the full catch whatever the volume [k], giving Saltpan a guaranteed outlet for the 24 tonnes a year that currently go through it [app], securing reliable weekly cash flow without finding 32 individual direct buyers [an]. Reason 2: Selling wholesale needs no van, extra staff or marketing [k], avoiding the $25,000 refrigerated van and the daily effort of chasing $22-per-kg restaurant orders [app], keeping overheads low and letting the 8 fishermen focus on fishing [an].

knowledge_max_2: a wholesale market guarantees an outlet for the entire catch
wholesale sales require no extra vehicle, staff or marketing spend
application_max_2: 24 tonnes a year (80% of 30 tonnes) currently go through the wholesale market
avoids the $25,000 refrigerated van and daily management of restaurant orders
analysis_max_2: guaranteed outlet secures consistent revenue and working capital
lower overheads let the business concentrate on fishing rather than distribution

questions.question_text: Do you think Saltpan Lobster Co should buy the refrigerated van and sell more lobsters directly to restaurants? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Buying the van would let Saltpan supply 20 more restaurants directly at $22 per kg [k]; shifting 6 tonnes a year from the wholesale rate to the direct rate would add about $48,000 of revenue (6,000 kg x $8 extra per kg) without catching more lobster [app]. Fresher deliveries would also build restaurant loyalty and justify premium menu pricing [an]. However, the van costs $25,000 and brings fuel, insurance and maintenance costs, and the direct channel only works if 20 restaurants order reliably every week [k]; dropped or forgotten orders would leave perishable stock worthless [app], and the wholesale market still guarantees an outlet for any unsold catch and pays reliably [an]. Overall, Saltpan should buy the van, because moving more volume to the $22-per-kg direct channel clearly beats $14 per kg for a freshness-critical product [eval], but only after the 20 restaurants commit to standing weekly orders, with the wholesale market kept as a fallback for unsold stock [eval].

knowledge_max_2: direct supply to restaurants commands a higher price for perishable seafood
however, it requires vehicle investment and reliable weekly ordering by buyers
application_max_2: shifting 6 tonnes from $14 to $22 per kg adds about $48,000 a year (6,000 kg x $8)
the van costs $25,000 and must serve 20 more restaurants reliably each week
analysis_max_2: higher margin and fresher delivery strengthen restaurant relationships and revenue per kg
if restaurants cancel or volumes vary, perishable stock is lost and the van becomes a fixed burden
evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation to buy the van only with confirmed standing weekly orders
balanced judgement retaining the wholesale market as an outlet for unsold stock

scenario_stem:
Tidemill Electrical is a private limited company running 2 independent electrical goods shops in country towns in Country X. Founded 15 years ago, it employs 26 staff. Revenue last year was $1.8 million, but sales have fallen 12% over 2 years as online discounters undercut its prices.

The directors could build a website with click-and-collect for $35,000 plus $1,500 a month to maintain, letting customers order online and collect in store. It stocks about 1,400 product lines from 3 national suppliers. An online rival sells a $700 television for $549. The alternative is to remain a specialist high street retailer: 70% of Tidemill's customers say expert advice and free installation of kitchen appliances are why they shop there, and installation earns $300,000 a year.

questions.question_text: Define 'click-and-collect'.
questions.model_answer: A service where a customer orders goods online and collects them in person from a shop or depot at a chosen time [2].

knowledge_max_2: order placed online, typically paid for in advance
goods collected in person from a shop or depot

questions.question_text: Explain two threats e-commerce poses to Tidemill Electrical.
questions.model_answer: Threat 1: Online discounters carry lower store overheads and can undercut high street prices [k], as the rival selling a $700 television for $549 shows, helping drive Tidemill's 12% sales fall over 2 years [app]. Threat 2: Customers who buy online skip the shop entirely [k], so Tidemill loses walk-in trade that supports its $300,000 a year of kitchen appliance installation business [app].

online buying removes the store visit, cutting walk-in trade for physical retailers
application_max_2: a $700 television sold online for $549 undercuts Tidemill's pricing

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits Tidemill Electrical could gain from a click-and-collect website.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Click-and-collect lets Tidemill sell online while still driving customers into its two country-town shops [k], protecting footfall and upselling the kitchen appliance installation that already earns $300,000 a year [app], defending revenue and margins [an]. Benefit 2: Click-and-collect removes home delivery costs and waiting times [k], making online buying attractive for heavy items such as televisions and washing machines at a running cost of only $1,500 a month [app], improving convenience and customer loyalty [an].

knowledge_max_2: click-and-collect combines online ordering with in-store collection

questions.question_text: Do you think Tidemill Electrical should invest in a click-and-collect website? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Investing in click-and-collect would let Tidemill compete online while keeping its two shops relevant [k]; at $35,000 build cost and $1,500 a month running cost, it is cheaper than losing 12% of a $1.8 million business, about $216,000 of revenue at risk [app], and it converts browsing into store visits where advice and installation can be sold [an]. However, Tidemill cannot match online prices such as $549 for a $700 television, so price-led buyers may still leave [k]; the website only works if stock is visible online and collection is easy, and at $18,000 a year running cost the system must win back meaningful volume [app], otherwise the investment becomes an expensive brochure [an]. Overall, Tidemill should invest, prioritising click-and-collect over price cuts because its differentiator, advice and installation valued by 70% of customers, cannot be copied by online rivals [eval], and it should review sales versus the $216,000 at risk after 12 months [eval].

application_max_2: $35,000 setup plus $1,500 a month ($18,000 a year) versus about $216,000 revenue at risk from a 12% fall on $1.8 million

scenario_stem:
Copperhole Bakery is a private limited company operating 4 bakery outlets across Country X. It employs 28 staff, generates $520,000 in annual revenue and sells its best-known sourdough loaf to around 3,500 customers each week. The owners are considering opening a fifth outlet in the Riverside district, 12 km from the nearest existing store, and have set aside $7,500 for market research. They want the business to be market-orientated, making what customers want rather than what the owners prefer.

The owners must decide between conducting their own primary research — a questionnaire posted to 400 Riverside households plus follow-up interviews with 30 residents — and buying a secondary research report on Country X bakery spending, priced at $3,000, alongside free government statistics on local household incomes. Internal records show sourdough sales rose 18% last year.

questions.model_answer: Reason 1: To find out whether Riverside residents actually want a new bakery [k] before committing $7,500 and signing a lease on the fifth outlet [app]. Reason 2: To discover what products and prices Riverside customers would prefer [k], so the new branch can sell items like its best-known sourdough loaf rather than the owners guessing demand [app].

knowledge_max_2: identify customer demand or needs before committing resources

Benefit 2: They can reach many respondents in writing at low cost [k], such as 400 households compared with only 30 face-to-face interviews [app], giving a larger evidence base to set alongside internal records showing sourdough sales rose 18% last year [an].

However, secondary sources are quicker and cheaper [k]; the $3,000 report and free government statistics on local household incomes [app] would arrive without weeks of fieldwork [an]. scenario_stem:
Keswick Outdoors Ltd is a private limited company selling camping and hiking equipment from 3 stores across Country X. It employs 45 full-time staff, generated $1.1 million in revenue last year, and camping stoves accounted for 22% of total sales. The marketing manager is planning the summer launch of a new lightweight stove, the Trailflame, aimed at weekend hikers aged 25–40, and wants evidence before committing to a $60,000 production run.

The manager must choose between two primary research methods: running 4 focus groups of 8 hikers each, costing $1,800 in total including refreshments and venue hire, or carrying out an observation of shopper behaviour at the camping aisles of its 3 stores over 6 weekends using a trainee researcher. A secondary market research report on the Country X outdoor equipment sector, priced at $4,500 from a national research agency, is also available for comparison.

Reason 2: To gather up-to-date information on what hikers look for in a stove [k], such as weight, price and features, since stoves already account for 22% of store sales [app].

Benefit 2: The moderator can probe unexpected opinions and ask follow-up questions [k], unlike a written questionnaire, helping Keswick explore hikers' reactions for $1,800 across all 4 groups [app] and refine the stove before launch [an].

scenario_stem:
Hallowdene Clothing Co is a private limited company manufacturing school uniforms and workwear in Country X. It employs 120 machinists in its main factory, generated $2.4 million in revenue last year and winter jackets account for 30% of total sales. The company wants to survey customers about a new winter jacket range for 2027 and has chosen a sample of 400 respondents from its database of 6,500 recent buyers.

The marketing manager, newly promoted from production, must decide between random sampling — selecting 400 names using a computerised random number generator — and quota sampling, choosing respondents to match the database profile of 55% female, 45% male and 40% aged over 50. The questionnaire will be posted with a prepaid reply envelope and costs $2,000 to print and post, and results will guide the winter range launch.

questions.question_text: Define 'quota sampling'.
questions.model_answer: Selecting a sample in which respondents are chosen to fill set quotas matching the characteristics of the target market, such as age and gender [2].

quotas match the characteristics of the target market such as age or gender

questions.question_text: Explain two factors that could affect the accuracy of Hallowdene Clothing's questionnaire results.
questions.model_answer: Factor 1: A low or biased response rate [k]; if only a fraction of the 400 chosen names reply, the views of 6,500 recent buyers will be poorly represented [app]. Factor 2: Leading or unclear questions can bias the answers [k]; if the questionnaire nudges respondents towards the new winter jacket range, the 30% winter jacket share of sales may appear more popular than it is [app].

knowledge_max_2: low or biased response rate reduces accuracy
leading or unclear questions bias the answers
application_max_2: sample of 400 chosen from 6,500 recent buyers

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of random sampling for this survey.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Every name in the database has an equal chance of selection [k], so the 400 chosen from 6,500 recent buyers by random number generator [app] are less likely to be biased by the sampler's personal preferences [an]. Benefit 2: It is simple and quick to administer [k]; generating the sample costs nothing extra beyond the $2,000 printing and postage [app], leaving budget to chase replies and raise the response rate that drives accuracy [an].

knowledge_max_2: every member of the population has an equal chance of selection
simple and quick to administer
application_max_2: $2,000 to print and post the questionnaire
analysis_max_2: avoids bias from the sampler's personal preferences
frees budget to chase replies and improve response rate

questions.question_text: Do you think Hallowdene Clothing should use quota sampling rather than random sampling for its questionnaire? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Quota sampling ensures the sample mirrors the target market [k]; choosing respondents to match the database profile of 55% female, 45% male and 40% aged over 50 [app] guarantees older buyers are heard, which pure chance might miss [an]. However, random sampling avoids interviewer bias in who is approached [k]; a random number generator applied to all 6,500 recent buyers [app] gives every customer an equal, impartial chance of selection [an]. Overall, quota sampling is the better choice for this winter jacket survey [eval] because buying habits differ sharply between these gender and age groups, so matching the profile matters more than statistical impartiality [eval].

scenario_stem:

It employs 65 staff at its creamery, generates $1.6 million in annual revenue and sells to 240 independent shops in 12 regions. The owners want to launch a dairy dessert aimed at children and are choosing between two research options.

Option one is a secondary market research report on the Country X dairy dessert sector, priced at $5,000, plus free government statistics on household spending and the owners' own internet research on rival brands. Option two is primary research: 500 questionnaires posted to households in 3 cities, costing $9,500 including printing, postage and analysis by an external firm. The owners worry that published secondary data may be out of date or not specific enough.

questions.question_text: Define 'secondary market research'.
questions.model_answer: The use of information that has already been collected by someone else, such as government statistics, internet sources, market research reports and internal records [2].

knowledge_max_2: information already collected by someone else

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Rushmere Creamery of using secondary market research.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Secondary data is cheap and quick to access [k]; government statistics are free and the report costs $5,000, far less than the $9,500 needed for primary fieldwork [app]. Benefit 2: It can show the size and trends of the whole dairy dessert sector [k] before Rushmere commits to producing a new dessert for its 240 independent shops [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of relying on secondary market research for this launch.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: Secondary data may not be specific to the new dairy dessert [k]; the report covers the whole Country X dairy dessert sector, not children's reactions to Rushmere's recipe [app], so decisions rest on general rather than tailored evidence [an]. scenario_stem:
Calloway Rods is a sole-trader fishing-rod workshop in Country X run by Sam Whitaker, building bespoke trout and salmon rods. Each rod is made to the angler's specification in about 7 days, sells at $340, and the workshop produced 260 rods last year with a 6-week waiting list and a part-time assistant who varnishes each rod.

Sam's supplier of hand-built cork grips has cut prices for identical grip designs ordered in batches. Local angling shops have asked to stock 3 standard models. Sam could keep full job production, switch the 3 standard models to batches of 40 and keep bespoke work on top, or go fully batch and drop custom orders completely, ending a decade of one-off builds. The shops want an answer within 3 months.

questions.question_text: Outline two advantages of batch production.
questions.model_answer: Batch production allows a range of different products to be made on shared machines, keeping some flexibility between runs [1]. Unit costs are lower than job production because larger quantities spread fixed and setup costs [1]. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Different products made in batches on shared machinery / flexibility of range
Lower unit cost than job production / setup costs spread over batch

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why batch production might help Calloway Rods.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Batch production lowers unit costs for standard lines [k]. Making 3 standard models in batches of 40 would spread labour and machine time across 120 rods, cutting average cost per rod compared with one-off builds [app]. Reason 2: Batch production can supply local angling shops reliably [k]. Stocking 3 standard models in predictable batches of 40 matches exactly what the shops have asked for and relieves the 6-week waiting list [app].

knowledge_max_2: Lower unit cost from larger runs / shared fixed costs
Predictable stock supply for retailers
application_max_2: 3 standard models x 40 = 120 rods per batch cycle
Angling shops asked for 3 standard models; 6-week waiting list

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Calloway Rods could face if it switched fully to batch production.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Unique bespoke work would disappear [k]. Dropping custom orders means giving up the $340 bespoke trout and salmon rods and the loyal customers behind the 6-week waiting list [app], shrinking the firm's premium reputation with serious anglers [an]. Problem 2: Batch production risks unsold stock [k]. If the 3 standard models do not sell in batches of 40, capital is tied up in rods that angling shops cannot shift [app], raising storage costs and waste if designs fall out of fashion [an].

knowledge_max_2: Loss of custom/bespoke work and premium reputation
Risk of unsold stock / capital tied up in batches
application_max_2: $340 bespoke trout and salmon rods; 6-week waiting list
3 standard models in batches of 40 held as stock
analysis_max_2: Eroding bespoke reputation reduces premium pricing power
Unsold batches tie up cash and raise storage/obsolescence costs

questions.question_text: Do you think Sam should switch the three standard models to batch production alongside the bespoke work? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Arguments for switching: producing 3 standard models in batches of 40 spreads setup costs, frees capacity for bespoke rods and shortens the 6-week waiting list [k]. Supplier discounts on identical hand-built cork grips ordered in batches cut material costs further [app]. The angling shops' request widens the market beyond the 260 rods sold last year [an]. Arguments against: splitting production could dilute the bespoke reputation that supports $340 pricing [k]. Batch runs of 40 unsold models tie up cash, and savings only materialise if grips are ordered for proven demand [app]. Overproducing one design would leave expensive unsold stock [an]. Overall, adding 3 standard batch models alongside bespoke work captures shop demand and supplier discounts without abandoning the firm's identity, so the partial switch is justified [eval]. However, Sam should keep batches small and monitor sell-through before expanding, protecting workshop flexibility [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Batch suits standard models / spreads setup costs, frees capacity
Risks: diluted bespoke identity, unsold stock, tied-up capital
application_max_2: Batches of 40 for 3 standard models; 6-week waiting list; 260 rods last year
Supplier discounts on identical cork grips; $340 bespoke price
analysis_max_2: Wider market and lower costs while retaining bespoke identity
Overproduction and reputation dilution risk if demand misjudged
evaluation_max_2: Conditional justified judgement favouring partial switch
Safeguard suggested: small batches and sell-through monitoring

scenario_stem:
Brackenhill Biscuits Ltd is a family-owned biscuit manufacturer in Country X that has produced shortbread and cream crackers for 11 years. Last year the business invested $480,000 in an automated wrapping and packing line using robotic arms, capable of sealing 120 packs per minute. The new equipment replaced 3 manual packing benches and 15 jobs. The owning family wants the business to stay cost-competitive against larger rivals importing cheaper biscuits.

Since the line began operating in March, output has risen from 38,000 to 52,000 packs per week, and faulty seals have fallen from 4% to 1% of packs. The operations manager estimates the investment will pay for itself in under 3 years, although the 15 redundant packers received only statutory pay and morale among the remaining 60 factory workers has dipped.

knowledge_max_2: Higher productivity/output per period
Improved and more consistent product quality or fewer errors
application_max_2: Line seals 120 packs per minute and weekly output rose from 38,000 to 52,000 packs

questions.model_answer: First, redundancies [k]: the business made 15 packers redundant, so they received only statutory pay [app], and lower morale among the remaining 60 factory workers could raise absenteeism and errors [an]. Second, high capital outlay [k]: $480,000 had to be spent before the estimated payback of under 3 years [app], so if weekly output falls short of 52,000 packs the family may struggle to recover the cost and stay competitive against imports [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Brackenhill Biscuits should invest in automated mixing and baking equipment as well? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes, further automation should raise productivity [k]; the packing line lifted output from 38,000 to 52,000 packs per week and cut faulty seals from 4% to 1% [app]; extending the same technology to mixing and baking could remove more errors, lower unit costs and keep biscuits cheaper than imports [an]. However, automation destroyed jobs [k]; this project cost $480,000, made the 15 redundant packers leave on statutory pay and soured morale among the remaining 60 factory workers [app]; repeating that scale of disruption in mixing and baking, where timing and temperature need judgement, could deepen absenteeism and hurt consistency [an]. Overall I recommend phased investment in automated mixing first, with skilled staff retrained and supervising [eval]; baking should keep human oversight for now, so automating both stages fully would be premature given the morale damage already seen [eval].

scenario_stem:
Cinderford Brickworks is a brick manufacturer in Country X that has supplied builders for 14 years, producing facing and engineering bricks for housebuilders across the region. Two years ago the owners spent $250,000 installing a mechanised extrusion machine and automatic wire-cutter, allowing operators to feed clay rather than mould bricks by hand. The yard now employs 74 workers, 30 of whom run the machines.

Output has risen from 140,000 to 210,000 bricks per week, and reject bricks have fallen from 7% to 3%. Hourly wages of $11.50 for machine operators tempt the business to recruit 6 more workers this year, but clay prices have climbed 12%. The kilns are now the production bottleneck, and the owners have delayed a planned wage rise until 2027 while they repay the machine loan.

questions.model_answer: First, to raise output [k]; the mechanised extruder and wire-cutter lifted production from 140,000 to 210,000 bricks per week [app]. Second, to cut waste [k]; reject bricks fell from 7% to 3% after the machines were installed [app].

knowledge_max_2: To increase output/productivity
To reduce waste, rejects and human error
application_max_2: Production rose from 140,000 to 210,000 bricks per week

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Cinderford Brickworks may face from its mechanisation.
questions.model_answer: First, dependence on skilled operators [k]: the business relies on 30 of its 74 workers to run the machines at $11.50 per hour [app], so any absence or breakdown could stop extrusion and widen the kiln bottleneck [an]. Second, rising input costs [k]: clay prices have climbed 12% [app], squeezing margins and making it harder to recover the $250,000 outlay without raising brick prices for builders [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Cinderford Brickworks should now invest in mechanising the kilns as well? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes, mechanising the kilns would attack the bottleneck [k]; the yard already lifted output from 140,000 to 210,000 bricks per week and cut rejects from 7% to 3% by mechanising extrusion [app]; applying the same approach to firing could raise capacity and stabilise quality while builder demand keeps growing [an]. However, machines reduce rather than increase labour needs [k]; the business has already spent $250,000 and pays operators $11.50 per hour amid a 12% clay price rise [app], and another large outlay plus recruiting 6 more workers risks overstretching cash if the housing market slows [an]. Overall I recommend phased kiln mechanisation funded largely from retained profit, because the proven 50% output gain outweighs the cost risk, provided the new recruits are trained to operate the machines before phase two begins [eval]; if clay costs keep climbing, phase two should be delayed rather than debt-financed [eval].

scenario_stem:
Halyard Lighting Co is a manufacturer of decorative ceiling lamps, wall lights and brass fittings in Country X, trading for 9 years. Its design team of 6 uses CAD software that cost $95,000 to create and modify lamp designs on screen before any prototype is built. Design revisions that once took 3 weeks can now be completed in 4 days.

Sales last year reached $2.1 million. Prototyping waste fell by 40%, but the finance director warns the software licence is due for renewal at $18,000 per year and two senior designers were hired on $42,000 salaries to run it. The board values the design edge CAD gives against copycat rivals, yet must now decide whether to buy 2 more CAD licences or hire another designer.

questions.model_answer: CAD is the use of computer software to create, modify and test product designs digitally before any prototype is built [2].

knowledge_max_2: Computer software is used to design products
Designs can be created, modified and tested digitally before manufacture

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Halyard Lighting of using CAD in its design work.
questions.model_answer: First, design speed improved [k]; revisions that once took 3 weeks can now be completed in 4 days [app]. Second, material waste fell [k]; prototyping waste dropped by 40% because errors are spotted on screen [app].

knowledge_max_2: Faster design and revision process
Reduced waste and errors before prototyping
application_max_2: Revisions completed in 4 days instead of 3 weeks

questions.question_text: Explain two costs or drawbacks of CAD for Halyard Lighting Co.
questions.model_answer: First, ongoing licence costs [k]: the software licence is due for renewal at $18,000 per year [app], so the $95,000 purchase is not a one-off cost and profits will be reduced every year [an]. Second, dependence on skilled staff [k]: two senior designers on $42,000 salaries were hired to run it [app], so the business faces retraining costs and disruption if they leave or the software is replaced [an].

Need for trained specialist staff and risk of dependency

Two senior designers hired on $42,000 salaries to run it

questions.model_answer: Yes, more licences extend a proven advantage [k]; CAD already cut design revisions from 3 weeks to 4 days and prototyping waste by 40% [app]; giving the existing design team of 6 more licences would let everyone work simultaneously, cutting revision queues and supporting the $2.1 million sales pipeline [an]. However, licences alone cannot originate ideas [k]; the licence costs $18,000 per year on top of $95,000 already spent, and two senior designers already earn $42,000 salaries [app]; another designer would add fresh creative capacity, share the workload at peaks and reduce over-reliance on the software [an]. Overall I recommend buying the 2 licences first, because the 4-day revision turnaround and 40% waste saving show CAD is delivering value [eval]; if design orders keep growing, hire a designer later rather than carry both costs at once [eval].

scenario_stem:
Dunmere Plastics Ltd is an injection-moulding business in Country X producing plastic housings for washing machines, lawnmowers and dishwashers, trading for 8 years. The factory runs two 8-hour shifts, five days a week. It recently installed CAM software costing $320,000 to control its 8 moulding machines directly from programs written by the production office. CAM programs also log every machine fault automatically.

Machine set-up time has fallen from 45 minutes to 12 minutes, and scrap has fallen from 9% to 4% of output. Annual output is now 950,000 housings, exported to 3 countries. Orders from 2 washing-machine plants account for 80% of output. The managing director is considering extending CAM to the final assembly robot, which would displace 12 of the 120 employees.

knowledge_max_2: Computer software controls machines/processes

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of CAM for Dunmere Plastics Ltd.
questions.model_answer: First, faster set-ups [k]; machine set-up time fell from 45 minutes to 12 minutes [app]. Second, less waste [k]; scrap fell from 9% to 4% of output [app].

knowledge_max_2: Reduced machine set-up/changeover time
Reduced scrap/waste and errors
application_max_2: Set-up time fell from 45 minutes to 12 minutes
Scrap fell from 9% to 4% of output

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Dunmere Plastics may face if it extends CAM to the final assembly robot.

Second, high extra cost and risk [k]: after spending $320,000 on moulding CAM, another system must be bought and integrated [app], so if exports to the 3 countries slow, the investment may take longer to repay and strain cash flow [an].

questions.model_answer: Yes, assembly CAM would compound the gains [k]; moulding CAM already cut set-ups from 45 to 12 minutes and scrap from 9% to 4%, with 950,000 housings exported to 3 countries [app]; extending computer control to assembly could deliver the same consistency at the final stage and help win larger export contracts [an]. However, assembly CAM would displace 12 of the 120 employees [app]; the moulding system already cost $320,000 [k], and forcing 12 redundancies could lower morale, raise absenteeism and increase long-run labour costs among those remaining [an]. Overall I recommend extending CAM to assembly only if the 12 affected workers are retrained or redeployed [eval]; the quality and export benefits justify the move, but rushing it without reskilling would risk the workforce goodwill the business still needs [eval].

scenario_stem:
Aldercroft Auto Components is a private limited company in Country X producing suspension brackets and exhaust flanges for 2 car assembly plants. It employs 240 workers at a single factory on an industrial estate. Two years ago the business invested $1.2 million in a CIM system linking its design office, 14 CNC machines, quality scanners and a stock control database.

The system passes CAD designs straight to CAM files, schedules machine use automatically and flags defects on the line. Defective brackets fell from 6% to 1.5%, and average lead time dropped from 21 to 9 days, helping both assembly plants cut buffer stock. However, CIM needs 2 full-time IT technicians on $38,000 salaries, and the $1.2 million was financed by a bank loan.

knowledge_max_2: Improved quality/fewer defects
Faster lead time/quicker deliveries
application_max_2: Average lead time dropped from 21 to 9 days

questions.model_answer: First, dependence on specialist staff [k]: CIM needs 2 full-time IT technicians on $38,000 salaries [app], so if they leave, the whole production line could stall until replacements are found and trained [an]. Second, financial risk [k]: the $1.2 million was financed by a bank loan [app], so the business must keep the 2 assembly plants' orders profitable enough to meet interest payments, or face cash-flow pressure if orders fall [an].

However, the first $1.2 million was financed by a bank loan and the system already needs 2 IT technicians on $38,000 salaries [app]; duplicating it doubles loan pressure, and one technical failure could halt even more limited IT capacity [an], even though integration usually lifts productivity [k]. scenario_stem:
Dorchester Village Stores operates 6 grocery supermarkets in Country X, employing 145 staff. Last year it spent $180,000 installing EPOS tills in all 6 stores. Each checkout now scans barcodes, records sales by the hour and updates a central stock database automatically. The head office believes EPOS will free staff from manual stock counts.

EPOS data shows fresh-food wastage fell from 12% to 7% of stock within 4 months. The system flags when any of 400 key product lines drop below 2 weeks of expected sales. Trading on a Saturday can reach $38,000 per store, so managers worry automatic orders may over-buy perishables before quiet weekdays. The board is debating whether EPOS should place automatic reorders or whether store managers should approve all orders above $5,000.

questions.model_answer: First, reduced wastage [k]; fresh-food wastage fell from 12% to 7% of stock within 4 months [app]. Second, better reordering [k]; the system flags when any of 400 key product lines drop below 2 weeks of expected sales [app].

Second, to balance wastage against availability [k]; fresh-food wastage fell from 12% to 7% after EPOS began tracking sales [app], showing that accurate stock data lets the business hold the right amount instead of over-ordering perishables [an].

questions.model_answer: Yes, automatic reorders match stock to real demand [k]; EPOS already cut fresh-food wastage from 12% to 7% and records sales hourly [app]; automatic replenishment of the 400 key lines below 2 weeks of expected sales would prevent stockouts on busy Saturdays, when each store can take $38,000 [an]. scenario_stem:
Tannersley Glassworks is a glass bottle manufacturer in Country X that has supplied soft-drink bottlers for 16 years. Its 120 workers produced 240,000 bottles per week, an average of 2,000 bottles per worker per week. After installing 2 new furnaces and an extra forming machine costing $900,000, the factory made 288,000 bottles per week with 96 workers. The factory operates three shifts, six days a week.

That equals 3,000 bottles per worker per week, a 50% rise in productivity, and annual output is now about 15 million bottles, up from 12.5 million. The $900,000 was borrowed from a bank. Overtime would cost $16 per hour time-and-a-half, while a furnace would take 18 months to install but last 25 years. Bottlers want an extra 40,000 bottles a week under contract.

questions.model_answer: Productivity is the output produced per worker, or per other input, over a given time period [2].

knowledge_max_2: Output per worker/per input

questions.question_text: Explain two differences between production and productivity.
questions.model_answer: First, what they measure [k]; production is total output, which rose from 240,000 to 288,000 bottles per week, while productivity is output per worker, which rose from 2,000 to 3,000 bottles per worker [app]. Second, how each is increased [k]; production can be raised by adding workers or overtime, while productivity rose because 96 workers replaced 120 after the new machines arrived [app].
