Production can be raised by more inputs; productivity by more efficient use of inputs
application_max_2: Total output rose from 240,000 to 288,000 bottles per week
Output per worker rose from 2,000 to 3,000 after the workforce fell from 120 to 96

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Tannersley Glassworks of the rise in productivity.
questions.model_answer: First, lower labour cost per bottle [k]; output rose from 240,000 to 288,000 bottles per week while the workforce fell from 120 to 96 [app], so fixed costs are spread over more units and the business can improve profit to help repay the $900,000 loan [an]. Second, stronger competitiveness [k]; each of the 96 remaining workers now produces 3,000 bottles per week [app], so unit costs fall and Tannersley can undercut rivals to win the contract for an extra 40,000 bottles a week [an].

knowledge_max_2: Higher output per worker lowers average cost per unit
Improved efficiency and competitiveness
application_max_2: Output rose 240,000 to 288,000 bottles per week while staff fell from 120 to 96
Each worker now produces 3,000 bottles per week
analysis_max_2: Fixed costs are spread over more bottles, improving profit and ability to repay the bank loan
Lower unit costs strengthen competitiveness and support winning the extra 40,000 bottles contract

questions.question_text: Do you think Tannersley Glassworks should raise output further by overtime or by buying a third furnace? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes, a third furnace would replicate the gains [k]; productivity already rose from 2,000 to 3,000 bottles per worker after the 2 new furnaces were installed [app]; a third furnace would last 25 years and help supply bottlers the extra 40,000 bottles a week under contract [an]. However, overtime is more flexible right now [k]; the $900,000 was borrowed and overtime at $16 per hour time-and-a-half adds capacity without new long-term debt [app]; but overtime raises labour cost per bottle and cannot match machine efficiency or consistent quality [an]. scenario_stem:
Breckfield Pump Works is a private limited company in Country X making water pumps for farms for 11 years. It employs 85 workers and produces 1,400 pumps a month. Annual sales revenue is $11.2 million. Errors between the design office and the factory floor mean 8% of pumps need reworking before dispatch.

The directors are choosing between two options. Option A is to keep the existing separate CAD and CAM machines with 2 standalone inspection stations. Option B is to spend $2.4 million on a CIM system linking the design office, 6 CNC machines, automated scanners and the stock control database, which would cut rework from 8% to 3% and raise output to 1,750 pumps a month. Training 12 staff would cost $36,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'computer-integrated manufacturing (CIM)'.
questions.model_answer: Computer-integrated manufacturing is the linking of all production stages - design, machining, quality inspection and stock control - into one computer-controlled system that shares information automatically. [2]

knowledge_max_2: CIM links design, production, inspection and stock in one computer system
Information flows automatically between stages without manual paperwork

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Breckfield Pump Works of installing a CIM system.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: CIM shares design data directly with the machines, removing manual re-entry [k]. Rework would fall from 8% of pumps to 3%, saving materials and labour [app]. Benefit 2: Linking all stages in one system speeds up the whole production flow [k]. Output would rise from 1,400 pumps a month to 1,750 pumps a month, a 25% increase [app].

knowledge_max_2: CIM removes manual data transfer errors between design and production
An integrated flow speeds up the process from planning to dispatch
application_max_2: Rework falls from 8% to 3% of pumps
Output rises from 1,400 to 1,750 pumps a month (a 25% increase)

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Breckfield Pump Works could face if it installs a CIM system.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: CIM costs a great deal of money up front [k]. Option B requires $2.4 million plus $36,000 to train 12 staff [app]. Borrowing that sum would add interest payments and raise financial risk for the company [an]. Problem 2: CIM depends on all its linked parts working together [k]. A fault in 1 of the 6 CNC machines or in the shared database could stop the whole line [app]. One breakdown could halt deliveries to farm customers and breach supply commitments [an].

It bottles fresh milk and plain yoghurt for 25 local shops, employs 18 workers and produced 200,000 litres last year. Fixed costs would rise only to $160,000, bulk buying of bottles and lids would cut variable costs by $0.05 per litre, and six extra staff would be needed. scenario_stem:
Thornfield Freight is a private limited company operating 9 HGVs in Country X, delivering to supermarkets and builders' merchants across two provinces. January inflows are forecast at $34,600 against outflows of $39,800, while February inflows are $44,300 against outflows of $38,200. The business was founded 7 years ago and begins January with an opening balance of $8,900, with current assets of $74,000 and current liabilities of $41,000.

Thornfield owes its diesel supplier $28,000, due in late February. Customers owe the freight firm $41,000, of which $19,000 is more than 60 days overdue. Marcus Vale, the managing director, must decide whether to delay the diesel payment by 30 days, press customers to settle the overdue $19,000 first, and postpone the $16,000 tyre replacement to April.

questions.question_text: Calculate the working capital for Thornfield Freight. Show your working.

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons for the negative net cash flow forecast in January.

Reason 2: customers pay late and do not cover the gap [k]; customers owe $41,000, of which $19,000 is more than 60 days overdue, so January inflows barely reflect work already done [app].

questions.question_text: Do you think Marcus should delay the diesel payment, or press customers to pay the overdue $19,000 first? Justify your answer.

scenario_stem:
Fenwick Refrigeration Ltd is a private limited company in Country X that services refrigeration units for supermarket and restaurant chains. Working capital is $170,000 and capital employed is $990,000. Non-current liabilities comprise a $300,000 long-term bank loan, so shareholders' equity is $690,000. scenario_stem:
Carrowmore Weavers Ltd is a private limited company in Country X weaving wool fabrics for made-to-measure tailoring businesses. Current assets total $208,000, including $120,000 owed by customers (one major customer settles around 60 days late) and inventories of $70,000. Current liabilities are $150,000, including $112,000 owed to suppliers, so working capital is $58,000. scenario_stem:

The statement of financial position shows non-current assets of $350,000, current assets of $160,000 (including cash of $55,000) and current liabilities of $70,000, giving working capital of $90,000 and capital employed of $440,000. Non-current liabilities are $120,000, so shareholders' equity is $320,000. questions.question_text: Define 'Shareholders' Equity'.

application_max_2: Existing $320,000 equity remains in the same hands

Point 2: Most of the current assets are tied up as $85,000 of inventories and $95,000 of trade receivables, leaving $10,000 of cash, so one slow-paying customer could create an immediate cash crisis [k][app][an].

Current assets dominated by inventories and receivables rather than cash signals weak liquidity

questions.question_text: Do you think the directors should cut inventories to $55,000 (Option 1) or ask the bank to convert the $60,000 overdraft into a long-term loan (Option 2)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option 1 releases about $30,000 of cash from inventories without new debt and reduces storage and spoilage costs on perishable cheese, but it does not by itself lift working capital above $40,000 [k][app][an]. Option 2 would cut current liabilities to $90,000, raising working capital to $100,000 and removing an overdraft repayable on demand, at the price of a longer commitment and interest [k][app][an]. Overall, Option 2 is the stronger recommendation because the statement of financial position reveals a structural shortfall of long-term finance rather than simply surplus stock; converting the overdraft restores a safe working capital position, and the released cash plus Option 1's efficiency gains would compound [eval][eval].

Converting short-term debt to long-term debt directly raises working capital
analysis_max_2: Option 1 improves cash and lowers waste but leaves the balance sheet fragile
Option 2 fixes the structural mismatch and removes on-demand repayment risk
evaluation_max_2: Against Option 2: interest and a longer commitment / against Option 1: stockouts risk losing orders

scenario_stem:
Hedgerow Launderette Ltd is a private limited company in Country X operating two high-street launderettes. In the year ended 31 July 2026 it recorded Revenue of $310,000, Cost of Sales of $96,000, Gross Profit of $214,000, Expenses of $139,000 and Profit for the year of $75,000, compared with $52,000 the previous year. All profit is retained and no dividend is paid.

The board is choosing between Option 1, opening a third launderette costing $150,000 funded from accumulated retained profits, and Option 2, keeping a $150,000 cash reserve in case the two existing shops suffer a downturn. The statement of financial position shows non-current assets of $280,000, current assets of $190,000 (including cash of $130,000) and current liabilities of $75,000. Working capital is $115,000, capital employed is $395,000, there are no non-current liabilities and shareholders' equity is $395,000.

questions.question_text: Outline why profit is important to a business.
questions.model_answer: Profit is the reward to owners for taking the risk of investing; it provides internal funds for growth, enables dividends to be paid and creates a cushion against future losses [2].

knowledge_max_2: Rewards owners/shareholders for the risk they take (return on investment)
Provides internal funds for growth and a buffer against losses

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits profit has brought Hedgerow Launderette Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Profit rose from $52,000 to $75,000, an increase of about 44%, showing the two shops are trading increasingly successfully [k][app]. Reason 2: Because no dividend is paid, all profit is retained — building the $130,000 cash balance and the $395,000 of shareholders' equity that could fund future growth [k][app].

knowledge_max_2: Profit can be retained to finance growth internally
Retained profit strengthens reserves, equity and the cash position
application_max_2: All profit retained, building $130,000 cash and $395,000 equity

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why profit figures alone cannot tell the board whether Option 1 is safe.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Profit is not cash — the company records $75,000 of annual profit but holds only $130,000 of cash, and the $150,000 cost of a third shop exceeds that balance [k][app][an]. Reason 2: Paying for Option 1 would drain working capital of $115,000, since current assets of $190,000 would no longer comfortably cover current liabilities of $75,000 once the cash is spent [k][app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Profit differs from cash — it is an accounting figure, not spendable money
Spending funds reduces liquidity shown in the statement of financial position
application_max_2: Working capital $115,000 and current assets $190,000 would be drained against $75,000 current liabilities
analysis_max_2: The board would need at least $20,000 of extra finance for the gap
After spending, the business could not absorb a downturn in either existing shop

questions.question_text: Do you think the board should open the third launderette now (Option 1) or build up a cash reserve (Option 2)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option 1 would extend a proven, profitable concept — Profit jumped to $75,000 — and would create a third income stream funded from accumulated retained profits rather than new debt [k][app][an]. Option 2 protects the position, keeping $130,000 of cash, $190,000 of current assets and working capital of $115,000 available if either existing shop suffers a downturn [k][app][an]. Overall, Option 2 is the more responsible decision now because Option 1 costs $150,000 against $130,000 of cash, so opening immediately would strain liquidity when current liabilities of $75,000 already absorb part of the assets; the board should build the reserve first and fund the third shop in a year or two from retained profits [eval][eval].

knowledge_max_2: Expansion can raise future profit if the concept is proven
Cash reserves protect the business against downturns
application_max_2: Option 2 preserves $190,000 current assets and $115,000 working capital
analysis_max_2: Option 1 risks liquidity strain and may need external finance
Option 2 forfeits early growth but guarantees the existing shops survive a shock
evaluation_max_2: Against Option 2: idle cash earns little and competitors may move first
Overall: Option 2 first — rebuild cash, then expand from retained profits

scenario_stem:
Tamarind Soap Co Ltd is a private limited company in Country X making handmade botanical soaps. In the year ended 31 May 2026 it recorded Revenue of $260,000, Cost of Sales of $92,000, Gross Profit of $168,000, Expenses of $118,000 and Profit for the year of $50,000. A national supermarket chain has offered a one-year contract to buy 40,000 bars at $1.50 each, adding $60,000 of Revenue in exchange for $38,000 of extra materials.

The directors are choosing between Option 1, accepting the supermarket contract, which would lift total Revenue to $320,000 and Gross Profit to $190,000, and Option 2, continuing boutique sales and developing a premium gift range expected to add $30,000 to Gross Profit at no extra capital cost. Current assets are $120,000, current liabilities are $48,000 and non-current assets are $300,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'Cost of Sales'.
questions.model_answer: Cost of sales is the direct cost of producing or purchasing the goods a business sells during the period, such as raw materials and direct labour [2].

knowledge_max_2: Direct costs directly linked to the goods/services sold
Examples: raw materials, components, direct labour

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of Tamarind Soap Co Ltd's high Gross Profit.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Gross Profit of $168,000 — about 65% of Revenue — comfortably covers Expenses of $118,000 and still leaves Profit of $50,000 [k][app]. Reason 2: A strong Gross Profit shows each product creates substantial added value, giving the business room to fund the premium gift range without external finance [k][app].

knowledge_max_2: High gross profit covers expenses and secures net profit
Shows products create real added value, enabling self-funding of projects
application_max_2: $168,000 gross profit vs $118,000 expenses leaves $50,000 profit
~65% margin gives headroom to fund the gift range internally

questions.question_text: Explain two implications of the supermarket contract for the income statement.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: Revenue would rise by $60,000 to $320,000, but Cost of Sales would rise by $38,000 too, so Gross Profit would reach only $190,000 [k][app][an]. Point 2: The contract earns just $22,000 of Gross Profit on $60,000 of Revenue — about 37%, well below the boutique margin — so the company's overall Gross Profit margin would fall even as total profit rises [k][app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Both revenue and cost of sales rise under a new contract; gross profit is the difference
A contract margin below the business average dilutes overall margin
application_max_2: Revenue $320,000 and Gross Profit $190,000 under Option 1
Contract contributes about $22,000 on $60,000 (~37% vs ~65% boutique margin)
analysis_max_2: Total profit rises while margin percentage falls — volume growth at low margin
Each contract sale generates less cash to cover Expenses and risk

questions.question_text: Do you think the directors should accept the supermarket contract (Option 1) or develop the premium gift range (Option 2)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option 1 guarantees Revenue of $320,000 and Gross Profit of $190,000, securing volume for the soap room and using spare capacity at low added capital cost [k][app][an]. Option 2 should add $30,000 of Gross Profit at the full boutique margin with no extra materials risk, lifting Gross Profit towards $198,000 while preserving exclusivity [k][app][an]. Overall, Option 2 is the better fit for this business because it protects the ~65% margin that defines the brand, requires no $38,000 materials outlay against current liabilities of $48,000, and keeps the premium positioning that supermarket own-label supply would gradually erode [eval][eval].

knowledge_max_2: Guaranteed volume raises revenue but at a lower margin
Developing premium lines protects brand and margin
application_max_2: Option 2: about $30,000 extra Gross Profit (towards $198,000) with no capital cost
analysis_max_2: Option 1 dilutes margin and brand positioning; needs extra materials cash
Option 2 preserves margin, requires no extra materials, sustains brand exclusivity
evaluation_max_2: Against Option 2: demand for a gift range is uncertain / Option 1 is guaranteed volume
Overall: Option 2 — margin and brand protection outweigh the safer-but-thinner contract

scenario_stem:
Hazelbeck Vegetables Co Ltd is a private limited company in Country X packing frozen mixed vegetables for supermarket own-label ranges. It employs 34 people across two packing lines. In the year ended 30 November 2026, Revenue was $900,000, Cost of Sales was $560,000 and Gross Profit was $340,000. Expenses of $300,000 included $70,000 of advertising and $85,000 of freezer electricity, leaving Profit for the year of only $40,000.

The directors are choosing between Option 1, cutting the advertising budget by $28,000, and Option 2, spending $32,000 on freezer insulation expected to reduce electricity costs by $24,000 a year. The statement of financial position so far shows current assets of $260,000, current liabilities of $130,000 and non-current assets of $400,000, so working capital is $130,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'Expenses'.
questions.model_answer: Expenses are the indirect running costs of a business not included in the cost of goods sold, such as rent, administrative wages, utilities and advertising [2].

knowledge_max_2: Indirect/overhead costs of running the business
Not part of cost of sales — e.g. utilities, administration, advertising

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Hazelbeck Vegetables Co Ltd's expenses are a concern.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Expenses of $300,000 absorb almost all of the $340,000 Gross Profit, leaving only $40,000 of profit and almost no room for error [k][app]. Reason 2: Two of the largest expenses — $70,000 of advertising and $85,000 of freezer electricity — may be controllable, so targeted cuts could protect profit without touching product quality or safety [k][app].

knowledge_max_2: Expenses consume gross profit, leaving minimal net profit
Large individual expenses may be controllable and reducible
application_max_2: $70,000 advertising and $85,000 electricity are specific targets

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the Option 1 and Option 2 proposals would improve the business.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: Cutting advertising by $28,000 under Option 1 would lift Profit from $40,000 to $68,000 with no capital outlay at all [k][app][an]. Point 2: Insulation under Option 2 cuts the $85,000 electricity bill by $24,000 a year, a saving that recurs every year after the one-off $32,000 cost, leaving Profit around $64,000 [k][app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Reducing expenses directly raises profit
One-off capital costs differ from recurring cost savings
application_max_2: Option 1 lifts Profit from $40,000 to $68,000 with no outlay
analysis_max_2: Option 1 is immediate, reversible and costless in cash terms
Option 2 has a lasting benefit though it needs $32,000 up front

questions.question_text: Do you think the directors should cut the advertising budget (Option 1) or invest in freezer insulation (Option 2)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option 1 raises profit to $68,000 immediately and needs no cash outlay, preserving the $130,000 of working capital when current liabilities of $130,000 already absorb half of current assets [k][app][an]. Option 2 costs $32,000 and saves only $24,000 a year, boosting profit less, but it protects the advertising that secures supermarket own-label listings and the $900,000 Revenue base [k][app][an]. Overall, Option 1 is the better short-term choice on the numbers — $28,000 a year saved at zero capital cost — but the board should first test how productive the advertising really is, since cutting it blindly could damage the contracts behind the entire Revenue [eval][eval].

knowledge_max_2: Direct cost cuts raise profit immediately with no investment
Investment can produce recurring savings but ties up cash
application_max_2: Option 1: +$28,000 profit per year, no outlay
Option 2: $32,000 cost for $24,000 a year saved
analysis_max_2: Option 1 is riskier to revenue if advertising drives listings; Option 2 is safer for sales
Option 2's recurring saving compounds, Option 1's saving may hit sales
evaluation_max_2: Against Option 1: could damage supermarket relationships and Revenue
Overall: Option 1, conditional on verifying advertising effectiveness first

scenario_stem:
Wrenmore Garage Ltd is a private limited company in Country X operating an independent car repair workshop, mainly servicing family cars and small vans. In the year ended 31 October 2026 it recorded Revenue of $780,000, Cost of Sales of $300,000, Gross Profit of $480,000, Expenses of $350,000 and Profit for the year of $130,000. A dividend of $50,000 was paid and $80,000 of profit was retained.

The statement of financial position shows non-current assets of $520,000, current assets of $230,000 (including inventories of $80,000) and current liabilities of $110,000. Working capital is $120,000 and capital employed is $640,000. Non-current liabilities are $200,000 and shareholders' equity is $440,000. The landlord has offered to sell the freehold of the workshop for $640,000; the board is choosing between Option 1, a further $550,000 long-term bank loan plus $90,000 of cash, and Option 2, continuing to rent at $60,000 a year.

questions.question_text: Define 'Retained Profit'.
questions.model_answer: Retained profit is the profit left in the business after dividends (and tax) have been paid, accumulated over time in reserves as part of shareholders' equity [2].

knowledge_max_2: Profit kept in the business after dividends/tax are paid
Accumulates in reserves within shareholders' equity

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why capital employed is a useful figure for anyone judging Wrenmore Garage Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Capital employed of $640,000 shows the total long-term funds invested in the business — non-current assets of $520,000 plus working capital of $120,000 [k][app]. Reason 2: Comparing Profit of $130,000 with capital employed of $640,000 indicates how effectively the invested funds are being used to generate returns for investors [k][app].

knowledge_max_2: Shows the total long-term finance invested (non-current assets + working capital)
Enables judging how effectively invested funds generate profit

questions.question_text: Explain two effects on the statement of financial position if the directors buy the freehold (Option 1).
questions.model_answer: Point 1: Non-current assets would rise by $640,000 to $1,160,000 and non-current liabilities by $550,000 to $750,000, so capital employed would rise to $1,190,000 [k][app][an]. Point 2: Using $90,000 of cash cuts current assets to $140,000 while current liabilities stay at $110,000, so working capital falls to just $30,000 — a very thin cushion [k][app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Buying property increases non-current assets and total assets
Financing the purchase with a loan increases non-current liabilities and capital employed
application_max_2: Cash −$90,000 leaves current assets $140,000 and working capital $30,000
analysis_max_2: The statement of financial position still balances: $1,190,000 employed = $750,000 loan + $440,000 equity
Working capital of $30,000 against $110,000 current liabilities leaves almost no short-term slack

questions.question_text: Do you think the directors should buy the freehold using the loan (Option 1) or continue to rent (Option 2)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option 1 secures the workshop for the long term, removes the risk of rent increases and turns the $640,000 freehold into a company asset, though non-current liabilities rise to $750,000 and working capital falls towards $30,000 [k][app][an]. Option 2 keeps $230,000 of current assets and $120,000 of working capital intact, avoids extra interest and preserves flexibility, but the $60,000 annual rent never builds ownership [k][app][an]. Overall, continuing to rent (Option 2) is the wiser short-term decision because Profit of $130,000 covers the rent comfortably, and the thin $30,000 of working capital after purchase would leave the garage unable to absorb a shock; the board can revisit buying once retained profits rebuild the cash position [eval][eval].

knowledge_max_2: Buying property builds ownership and fixes premises cost long term
Renting preserves liquidity and flexibility but builds no asset
application_max_2: Option 1: non-current liabilities rise to $750,000; working capital about $30,000
Option 2: keeps $230,000 current assets and $120,000 working capital
analysis_max_2: Option 1 adds ownership and stability but concentrates risk in a thinner liquidity position
Option 2 avoids interest and preserves cash, but rent is a permanent cost with no equity built
evaluation_max_2: Against Option 2: rent never converts to ownership and may rise
Overall: Option 2 now — rebuild cash from retained profits, then buy later

scenario_stem:
Marlbrook Outfitters is a private limited company operating 3 clothing stores in Country X, run by managing director Naomi Hargrave for 8 years. In the year to 30 June, revenue was $840,000, cost of sales $462,000, gross profit $378,000, operating expenses $252,000 and profit $126,000; last year revenue was $780,000, gross profit $304,200 and profit $97,500 on a smaller range of premium lines.

Naomi is considering launching a cheaper own-brand clothing range to lift sales and compete with value retailers, or keeping the premium lines her loyal customers prefer. She has asked her accountant to prepare ratio analysis comparing both years for the board, which meets in 6 weeks to approve the own-brand range and decide its pricing and promotion.

questions.question_text: Define 'gross profit margin'.
questions.model_answer: Gross profit margin is the percentage of revenue remaining as gross profit after deducting the cost of sales, calculated as gross profit divided by revenue multiplied by 100; for Marlbrook Outfitters this year, $378,000 divided by $840,000 multiplied by 100 gives 45.0%, up from 39.0% last year. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Gross profit margin = gross profit / revenue x 100
It shows the percentage of each dollar of revenue kept after cost of sales

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Naomi should use gross profit margin when judging the own-brand proposal.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: gross profit margin shows the percentage of revenue left after the cost of sales, so it reveals how efficiently Marlbrook buys or makes its goods [k]; the margin improved from 39% ($304,200 divided by $780,000) last year to 45% ($378,000 divided by $840,000) this year, evidence that cost control on premium lines is strong [app]. Reason 2: gross profit margin lets Naomi compare lines and judge whether a cheaper own-brand range would still cover the cost of sales [k]; if the range runs near the current 45% margin while revenue passes $840,000, it adds profitable sales rather than diluting margins [app].

knowledge_max_2: Gross profit margin shows profitability after cost of sales, before expenses
Gross profit margin can be compared across periods or product lines to judge cost control
application_max_2: Applies last year's 39% from $304,200 / $780,000 and weighs margin against $840,000 revenue

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using gross profit margin alone to judge the own-brand proposal.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: gross profit margin ignores operating expenses [k]; with expenses of $252,000, the profit margin is only 15% ($126,000 divided by $840,000), so judging the range on the $378,000 gross profit alone could approve a proposal that actually cuts final profit [app][an]. Limitation 2: gross profit margin is calculated from historic figures and ignores other evidence [k]; last year's $304,200 and this year's $378,000 say nothing about how customers respond to cheaper own-brand clothing in one of the 3 stores, so sales and cash forecasts must also be studied [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Gross profit margin ignores expenses / overhead costs
Gross profit margin is historic and ignores non-financial evidence
application_max_2: Applies $252,000 expenses to show profit margin is only 15% ($126,000 / $840,000)
Applies historic figures such as $304,200 and $378,000 and the 3 stores context
analysis_max_2: Explains a proposal can raise gross profit yet cut final profit once expenses are charged
Explains historic margins cannot predict customer response to the cheaper range

questions.question_text: Do you think Naomi should launch the cheaper own-brand range? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Naomi could launch the range because demand from price-sensitive customers is often strong in clothing retail [k]. Revenue growing from $780,000 to $840,000 with a 45% gross profit margin shows Marlbrook can price own-brand lines below the premium tier and still cover the cost of sales, potentially lifting volume and profit together [app][an]. However, expenses of $252,000 leave a profit margin of only 15% ($126,000 divided by $840,000), so heavy discounting on the own-brand range could cut overall profit even as sales rise [app][an]. Conversely, keeping premium lines protects the margin gain from 39% to 45% and the rise from $97,500 to $126,000, but cedes the value segment to rivals [k][eval]. Overall, Naomi should trial the own-brand range in one of the 3 stores for one quarter, comparing its margin against 45% before wider roll-out; expand only if final profit holds above this year's $126,000, because the thin 15% profit margin leaves little room for error [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Gross profit margin improved from 39% to 45%; profit margin is 15% ($126,000 / $840,000)
Revenue grew from $780,000 to $840,000; expenses remain high at $252,000
application_max_2: Applies the 45% margin headroom and 15% profit margin to the range pricing decision
Applies revenue growth from $780,000 to $840,000 as evidence of demand
analysis_max_2: Explains that value demand and margin headroom could lift volume and profit together
Explains that discounting could cut final profit even if sales rise because expenses are fixed at $252,000
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation weighing margin protection against new demand, tied to a one-store trial and the $126,000 profit benchmark

scenario_stem:
Halvern Castings Ltd is a private limited company founded 9 years ago by Marcus Bellamy, casting iron brackets for farm machinery in a Country X factory employing 46 workers. At 30 June it held current assets of $286,000, comprising inventories of $150,000, trade receivables of $96,000 and cash of $40,000, against current liabilities of $104,000 to suppliers and the bank.

The main steel supplier has offered a 2% cash discount if Halvern settles the $60,000 early rather than on the usual 60-day terms. Marcus is deciding whether to take a 90-day bank loan at 1.5% interest to pay early, or to wait for the normal settlement date and risk upsetting the supplier before steel prices in Country X rise again next quarter.

questions.question_text: Define 'current ratio'.
questions.model_answer: The current ratio measures whether a business can meet its current liabilities with its current assets, calculated as current assets divided by current liabilities; Halvern Castings holds $286,000 of current assets against $104,000 of current liabilities, a ratio of 2.75:1. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities
It shows the liquidity of the business, i.e. its ability to pay short-term debts

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Marcus should check the current ratio before taking the loan.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: the current ratio shows whether current assets cover current liabilities [k]; Halvern's $286,000 of current assets against $104,000 of current liabilities is 2.75:1, indicating comfortable cover today before taking on a 90-day loan [app]. Reason 2: the current ratio helps Marcus see whether paying $60,000 early still leaves the business able to meet its remaining bills [k]; paying early would use the $40,000 cash plus part of the $96,000 trade receivables, so he must confirm cover stays above 1:1 through the 90 days [app].

knowledge_max_2: Current ratio shows whether current assets cover current liabilities
Current ratio indicates the liquidity buffer available before taking on new short-term debt
application_max_2: Applies the $40,000 cash and $96,000 trade receivables against the $60,000 early payment

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using the current ratio alone for this decision.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: the current ratio treats all current assets as equally quick to convert into cash [k]; Halvern holds $150,000 of inventories, the slowest asset, so excluding them (the acid test ratio) gives a more cautious picture of ($286,000 minus $150,000) divided by $104,000, about 1.31:1 [app][an]. Limitation 2: the current ratio is a single snapshot at 30 June and ignores timing [k]; if $96,000 of trade receivables pay slowly, Halvern may not have the $60,000 in cash even though the 2.75:1 ratio looks strong, so cash-flow timing must also be checked [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Current ratio assumes all current assets convert to cash equally fast
Current ratio is a static snapshot and ignores cash-flow timing
application_max_2: Applies the $150,000 inventories exclusion giving an acid test of about 1.31:1
Applies the $96,000 trade receivables timing and the 2.75:1 snapshot
analysis_max_2: Explains inventories are the slowest asset so the current ratio overstates true liquidity
Explains that a strong snapshot figure can still hide a cash-timing shortfall in the 90 days

questions.question_text: Do you think Marcus should take the 90-day bank loan to pay the supplier early? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Marcus could take the loan because a strong steel supplier supports reliable deliveries for the farm-machinery brackets his factory casts [k]. The 2% discount on the $60,000 saves $1,200 against $900 of interest (1.5% for 90 days), a net gain of $300, and the current ratio of 2.75:1 plus an acid test of about 1.31:1 shows he can cover a short 90-day loan from $286,000 of current assets [app][an]. However, the cash buffer is only $40,000 and the $96,000 of trade receivables must convert to cash within 90 days, so if customers pay late the loan rolls over with fresh interest and the net gain turns into a loss [app][an]. Conversely, waiting for the normal 60-day settlement costs nothing but forfeits the $1,200 discount and leaves the supplier waiting [k][eval]. Overall, Marcus should take the loan only if receivables have a strong payment record and the supplier confirms the terms in writing; the acid test of about 1.31:1 supports it, but with only a $300 net saving he should walk away if any part of the arrangement looks uncertain [eval].

knowledge_max_2: 2% discount on $60,000 = $1,200 saved; 1.5% for 90 days = $900 interest; net $300
Current ratio 2.75:1; acid test about 1.31:1; cash buffer only $40,000
application_max_2: Applies the $1,200 saving versus $900 interest and net $300 gain
Applies the $40,000 cash and $96,000 receivables against the 90-day repayment window
analysis_max_2: Explains receivables converting on time is essential or the loan rolls over costing more
Explains the liquidity ratios support a short-term loan from current assets
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation tied to written confirmation, receivables' payment record and the thin $300 net benefit

scenario_stem:
Tidewater Leisure Pools Ltd is a private limited company operating 2 swimming and fitness venues in Country X, directed by Rachel Achebe for 6 years. In the year to 31 August, profit was $180,000 and capital employed was $900,000; last year profit was $135,000 with capital employed of $900,000, and a nearby competitor achieves an ROCE of 12% across its larger chain of 4 venues.

Rachel must decide whether to build a third venue costing $400,000 from retained profit, expected to add only $52,000 in the first year but $112,000 once fully established, or to increase dividends of $60,000 a year payable to shareholders who have supported the company since it floated 6 years ago. The decision will be announced at the annual general meeting in September.

questions.question_text: Calculate the Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) for Tidewater Leisure Pools. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: ROCE is the percentage return a business earns on the capital invested in its operations, calculated as profit divided by capital employed multiplied by 100; Tidewater Leisure Pools earns $180,000 divided by $900,000 multiplied by 100 = 20.0% this year, up from 15.0% last year ($135,000 divided by $900,000 multiplied by 100). [2]

knowledge_max_2: ROCE = profit / capital employed x 100
It shows how effectively capital is used to generate profit

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why ROCE is the key figure for the board's decision.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: ROCE shows how much profit each dollar of capital employed generates [k]; Tidewater's ROCE improved from 15% last year ($135,000 divided by $900,000) to 20% this year ($180,000 divided by $900,000), well above the competitor's 12%, evidence that the existing venues earn strong returns [app]. Reason 2: ROCE lets the board compare the $400,000 third venue with leaving retained profit idle or paying dividends [k]; if the new venue lifts annual profit towards $292,000 in its third year, ROCE would reach about 22.5% ($292,000 divided by $1,300,000), beating the competitor and justifying the build [app].

scenario_stem:
Fallowfield & Dean Licensed Grocers Ltd is a private limited company running 2 convenience stores in Country X, owned by cousins Priya and Danny Fallowfield. In the year to 30 April, revenue was $800,000, gross profit $304,000, expenses $232,000 and profit $72,000; capital employed was $960,000 and current assets of $288,000 included inventories of $128,000, against current liabilities of $160,000.

The cousins want a $350,000 bank loan at 9% interest to refit both stores, improve refrigeration and add a chilled food counter. Alternatively, they could refit slowly over 3 years from retained profit. The bank has asked for ratio analysis from their accountant before deciding whether to approve the loan for the full amount requested. The cousins must satisfy the bank's lending committee in December.

questions.question_text: Identify two uses of ratio analysis.
questions.model_answer: Two uses of ratio analysis are firstly to compare a business's performance over time and against competitors, and secondly to support applications for finance such as bank loans by showing lenders the business's profitability and liquidity. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Ratio analysis compares performance over time or against competitors
Ratio analysis supports decisions and finance applications by quantifying profitability and liquidity

questions.question_text: Explain two ways ratio analysis can support the bank loan application.
questions.model_answer: Use 1: ratio analysis gives the bank a standardised view of creditworthiness [k]; the current ratio of 1.8:1 ($288,000 divided by $160,000) and an acid test ratio of 1.0:1 show the stores can cover short-term debts, supporting the $350,000 loan request [app]. Use 2: ratio analysis shows the owners understand their business numbers [k]; a gross profit margin of 38.0% ($304,000 divided by $800,000) and a 7.5% ROCE ($72,000 divided by $960,000) give the bank evidence the stores are profitable and professionally run [app].

knowledge_max_2: Ratio analysis provides standardised evidence of creditworthiness
Ratio analysis demonstrates the owners understand their business performance
application_max_2: Applies the 1.8:1 current ratio and 1.0:1 acid test ratio ($288,000, $128,000, $160,000)
Applies the 38.0% gross profit margin and 7.5% ROCE ($304,000 / $800,000; $72,000 / $960,000)

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of ratio analysis the cousins should consider.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: ratio analysis is based on historic accounts and cannot prove the refit will pay back [k]; a 9.0% profit margin ($72,000 divided by $800,000) would fall to about 5.1% after paying $31,500 of interest on the $350,000 loan (leaving $40,500 of profit), squeezing margins exactly when the stores need cash for the chilled counter [app][an]. Limitation 2: ratio analysis ignores qualitative factors and context [k]; neither the 38.0% gross profit margin nor the 1.8:1 current ratio captures customer loyalty, staffing stability or whether a chilled counter would actually lift sales, so the business plan matters as much as the figures [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Ratio analysis is historic and cannot prove future returns on investment
Ratio analysis ignores qualitative factors such as customers and staff
application_max_2: Applies the 9.0% margin falling to about 5.1% after $31,500 interest ($40,500 profit)
Applies the 38.0% gross profit margin and 1.8:1 current ratio ignoring loyalty and the chilled counter

questions.question_text: Do you think the cousins should take the bank loan? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The cousins could take the loan because refitting both stores now, rather than over 3 years from retained profit, defends the 38.0% gross profit margin ($304,000) against rivals adding chilled counters and captures sales sooner [k][app]. Profit of $72,000 (9.0% margin) barely covers the $31,500 interest, leaving $40,500 (5.1%), so the refit must generate meaningful new sales to be worthwhile [an]. However, the acid test ratio of 1.0:1 leaves no slack for trading setbacks, and capital employed would rise to $1,310,000, cutting ROCE to about 3.1% ($40,500 divided by $1,310,000) unless profits recover quickly [app][an]. Conversely, refitting slowly from retained profit avoids interest entirely and keeps the 1.0:1 acid test intact, but it cedes competitive advantage for 3 years and may never deliver the chilled food counter at all [k][eval]. Overall, the cousins should take the loan only if the bank offers a grace period before full repayments begin, because a 5.1% post-interest margin leaves almost no room for error; otherwise they should refit from retained profit and accept the slower refit as the safer route [eval].

evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation tied to a bank grace period, otherwise slower retained-profit refit

scenario_stem:
Wexcombe Pottery Ltd is a private limited company in Country X, founded 12 years ago and employing 58 workers at its Stokeham workshop. Staff belong to the Clay & Ceramics Union, which has tabled a 6% pay claim after the published final accounts showed revenue of $2.4 million, up from $2.1 million, and profit of $310,000, up from $185,000 a year earlier. The directors have countered with a 2% offer.

Union representatives want to inspect the full final accounts before talks, arguing the figures prove the claim is affordable. Managing Director Priya Nair must decide between granting 6%, costing the business an extra $96,000 a year, and holding to 2%, costing $32,000 and releasing funds for a kiln replacement. The annual wage bill is $1.6 million.

Profit rose to $310,000 on revenue of $2.4 million, so members argue the accounts prove the case for higher pay [app]. Second, the union uses the accounts to judge job security [k]. If profit fell back towards $185,000 or expenses spiked, jobs and future rises could be at risk, shaping whether to press for 6% or accept the $32,000 offer [app].

questions.model_answer: First, agreeing the claim raises wage costs [k]. The extra $96,000 a year would come from profit of $310,000, leaving only about $214,000 before tax [app]. This squeezes the owners' return and could force price rises, risking orders from price-sensitive retailers [an]. Second, the claim absorbs funds for the kiln replacement [k]. The 2% offer costs $32,000, but 6% costs $96,000, a difference of $64,000 [app]. Without the new kiln, output and quality at Stokeham could deteriorate, hurting delivery reliability and customer trust [an].

It costs $96,000 a year, and with profit of $310,000 the business could pay it while keeping about $214,000, improving morale across all 58 workers and cutting the risk of strikes [app]. Better motivation could lift output and reduce labour turnover at the workshop, protecting revenue of $2.4 million [an]. However, the 6% claim absorbs the funds needed for the kiln replacement, unlike the 2% offer costing $32,000 [k]. Accepting 6% would also set a precedent the business cannot afford if profit falls back towards $185,000 [app]. Sustained higher wages could force price rises that lose customers to rivals, eroding the very profit that makes the claim affordable [an]. Overall, I think Wexcombe Pottery Ltd should hold to the 2% offer plus a one-off profit-linked bonus [eval]. scenario_stem:
Aldergate Cycle Works Plc manufactures and sells bicycles across Country X from its Denham factory, employing 340 people, and is listed on the Country X Stock Exchange with about 420 shareholders. For the year just ended, revenue was $24 million and profit was $2.6 million on capital employed of $18.6 million, a return on capital employed of 14%, up from 11% two years ago.

The board plans a $2.2 million assembly hall. Under Option A, it pays an unchanged 6c dividend on the 10 million shares in issue, costing $600,000, leaving $2.0 million from profit; the $200,000 shortfall would be borrowed at 9% interest. Under Option B, the dividend is cut to 4c, costing $400,000, and the hall is funded entirely from retained profit.

questions.question_text: Define 'dividend'.
questions.model_answer: A dividend is a payment made by a company to its shareholders out of profits, usually expressed per share held, as a return on their investment [2].

knowledge_max_2: Payment made to shareholders out of profits

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why shareholders would use the final accounts of Aldergate Cycle Works Plc.
questions.model_answer: First, shareholders use the accounts to judge whether the profit can support dividends [k]. Profit of $2.6 million covers the unchanged 6c dividend of $600,000, and ROCE of 14%, up from 11% two years ago, signals the business is using its capital well [app]. Second, shareholders use the accounts to assess the risk and growth prospects of their investment [k]. With revenue of $24 million and capital employed of $18.6 million, and the board planning a $2.2 million assembly hall, investors can judge future returns and decide between the 6c and 4c dividend options [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Aldergate of funding the assembly hall from retained profit rather than borrowing.
questions.model_answer: First, funding from retained profit avoids interest charges [k]. Option B retains the full $2.2 million after a $400,000 dividend, whereas Option A leaves only $2.0 million and borrows $200,000 at 9%, costing about $18,000 a year in interest [app]. Avoiding that cost directly improves profit and frees up cash for tooling and maintenance in the new hall [an]. Second, retained profit avoids new debt and keeps control with existing shareholders [k]. Cutting the dividend to 4c funds the hall without loans or security, and shareholders keep ownership of a business whose ROCE is already 14% [app]. Lower debt levels reduce financial risk and protect independence, supporting the share price on the Country X Stock Exchange [an].

However, many shareholders rely on dividend income, and cutting the payout by a third may prompt some to sell, depressing the share price [k]. Others would prefer Option A's unchanged $600,000 payout with a modest $200,000 loan, accepting $18,000 annual interest to keep income stable [app]. Heavy selling could signal weak confidence and push the share price down, wiping out the income slowdown [an]. Overall, I think shareholders should approve the 4c dividend [eval]. scenario_stem:
Ternhill Dairy Ltd is a private limited company in Country X, founded 9 years ago, which makes cheese and butter and supplies 14 regional supermarkets. It employs 46 staff and has applied to Country X Bank for a $400,000 loan to buy three refrigerated delivery vans. Last year it reported revenue of $5.1 million and profit of $420,000.

The statement of financial position shows current assets of $980,000, including inventories of $350,000 and debtors of $520,000, against current liabilities of $600,000. The current ratio has fallen to 1.63 from 1.9 two years ago, and the acid test ratio has fallen to 1.05 from 1.3. Cash at bank is $110,000 and the loan application is with the credit manager this week.

questions.question_text: Define 'liquidity'.
questions.model_answer: Liquidity is the ability of a business to pay its short-term debts as they fall due, using cash or assets that can quickly be turned into cash [2].

knowledge_max_2: Ability to pay short-term debts as they fall due
Using cash or assets quickly convertible to cash

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Country X Bank would examine Ternhill Dairy Ltd's statement of financial position before granting the loan.
questions.model_answer: First, the bank wants to judge whether short-term debts can be paid [k]. Current assets of $980,000 against current liabilities of $600,000 give a current ratio of 1.63, down from 1.9 two years ago, which tells the bank Ternhill has some cushion but a weakening one [app]. Second, the bank wants to know what can be turned into cash quickly [k]. With inventories of $350,000 the acid test ratio is 1.05, down from 1.3, and cash is only $110,000, so the bank would probe the $520,000 of debtors to see whether supermarkets pay on time [app].

knowledge_max_2: Judge ability to pay short-term debts
Assess how much is quickly convertible to cash

Reference to acid test 1.05 vs 1.3; inventories $350,000, debtors $520,000, cash $110,000

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using the current ratio and the acid test ratio to judge Ternhill's ability to repay the loan.
questions.model_answer: First, ratios are a snapshot at one date [k]. Ternhill's current ratio of 1.63 and acid test ratio of 1.05 held at the year end, but a single late supermarket payment or a big stock delivery could change both quickly, so the figures may flatter the business on the day the $400,000 loan is decided [app]. Liquidity could be materially weaker exactly when the first instalments fall due [an]. Second, ratios ignore the quality of what the business owns [k]. Of the $980,000 of current assets, $350,000 is inventories and $520,000 is debtors; slow-paying or defaulting supermarkets, or damaged stocks, would shrink the real acid test well below 1.05 [app]. The bank could lend on the strength of figures that evaporate once debtors and inventories are properly valued [an].

knowledge_max_2: Ratios are a snapshot at one date; figures change quickly
Ratios ignore the quality of assets (stock and debtors may be impaired)

questions.question_text: Do you think Country X Bank should grant the $400,000 loan? Justify your answer.

Revenue of $5.1 million and supply deals with 14 regional supermarkets suggest steady cash generation, and three refrigerated vans would cut spoilage and secure deliveries, supporting future sales [app]. Stronger distribution could widen margins and lift profit further, improving the bank's repayment prospects across the term of the loan [an]. However, liquidity is weakening: the current ratio has fallen from 1.9 to 1.63, the acid test from 1.3 to 1.05, cash is only $110,000 and debtors are $520,000 — more than half of current assets [k]. Granting cash before debtors are collected could leave Ternhill unable to meet early instalments, especially if one supermarket pays late [app]. A rushed approval could turn a good customer into an overdraft problem, adding risk and cost to the bank with no extra margin [an]. Overall, I think Country X Bank should grant the loan, but in staged instalments linked to milestones, with vans delivered and debtors collected down to agreed limits [eval]. The profit and revenue justify supporting the business, yet the weakening acid test and $110,000 cash balance demand controls rather than one upfront payout [eval].

A new customer, Hollowbrook Homes Ltd, a housing developer, wants to buy $180,000 of materials for a 24-house estate and asks for 60 days to pay.

scenario_stem:
Stonemere Haulage Ltd is a private limited company in Country X, based at the Kinwell depot and the Northgate satellite yard, running 9 lorries for food and retail clients. It employs 34 drivers and warehouse staff. The government has announced grants covering 40% of the cost of electric trucks, provided applicants show two consecutive profitable years and create 3 new jobs per truck purchased.

Stonemere wants to buy 3 electric trucks at $160,000 each, totalling $480,000. Retained profit stands at $500,000 and the last two years produced profits of $175,000 and $210,000. The grant would contribute $192,000, leaving Stonemere to fund $288,000, but accepting it would oblige Stonemere to keep 9 new drivers for 3 years, publish its accounts annually and meet government reporting requirements.

Second, the agency must judge whether the promised jobs will last [k]. [k] With revenue of $14.2 million, extra borrowing at this point would still cut profit, especially if corporation tax rises from 24% to 28%. [app] Higher fixed costs from a third plant must be paid even if orders fall, so the break-even point rises and profit becomes more fragile. [an] Problem 2: When the boom ends, demand for bricks falls; a new plant built now may be underused, leaving excess capacity and heavy fixed costs. [k] Orders are full for the next 12 months, but the business cycle will eventually move into a slowdown, and the extra workers taken on cannot be avoided easily. [app] Underused capacity spreads fixed costs over fewer bricks, raising average costs and reducing competitiveness. [an]

Identifies that demand will fall when the boom ends, leaving excess capacity

questions.question_text: Do you think Coppermere Brick and Cement Co should invest $3 million in a third plant now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes: in a boom, demand is strong and delaying expansion means losing orders to rivals. [k] Revenue has already climbed from $11.8 million to $14.2 million and the order book is full for 12 months, so more capacity is needed urgently. [app] A third plant would let the firm serve all its housing-developer customers and raise profit despite the possible rise in corporation tax from 24% to 28%. [an] However, booms do not last forever; the business cycle will eventually turn to a downturn. [k] If the economy slows after the boom, the third plant's $3 million cost and the wages of extra workers would leave the firm with excess capacity and weaker cash to pay its 180 workers. [app] Delaying expansion until the boom ends would reduce this risk but would hand orders to competitors at the peak of demand. [an] Overall, the board should invest in the third plant now but phase the building over 18 to 24 months, keeping a cash reserve in case the cycle turns, because the revenue evidence strongly justifies expansion. [eval] This is justified by the $2.4 million revenue increase and the full order book; phasing the spend limits the damage if the boom ends sooner than expected. [eval]

Identifies that the boom will end and demand will fall (cycle risk)

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Marlowe & Grey Fine Watches is a partnership in Country X selling luxury watches and jewellery from 2 boutiques. It employs 14 specialist sales staff. Average takings per boutique fell to $95,000 a month in the latest quarter, down from $130,000 a year earlier, as Country X entered a slump. Footfall has fallen by a third since the slump began, and two nearby luxury retailers have closed.

Consumer confidence is very low and sales of luxury goods have dropped sharply. To help the economy, the government has cut VAT from 20% to 15% for 12 months. The partners must decide whether to cut prices by 10% to attract cautious buyers, or keep prices unchanged to protect the exclusive image of the brand.

questions.question_text: Define 'slump'.
questions.model_answer: A slump is the lowest point of the business cycle, when economic activity, output, incomes and employment are at their weakest and consumer spending is very low. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies the slump as the lowest/weakest stage of the business cycle
Identifies very low output, incomes, employment and/or consumer spending

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why sales of luxury watches and jewellery fall during a slump.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: In a slump, consumer incomes and confidence are very low, so households postpone non-essential high-price purchases such as luxury watches. [k] This is shown by takings per boutique falling from $130,000 to $95,000 a month. [app] Reason 2: In a slump, people fear for their jobs, so they prioritise essentials over luxury goods. [k] Footfall has fallen by a third and two nearby luxury retailers have closed, confirming the collapse in demand. [app]

Identifies job insecurity/fear of unemployment causing postponement of big non-essential purchases
application_max_2: References takings falling from $130,000 to $95,000 per boutique a month
References footfall falling by a third / two nearby luxury retailers closing

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of cutting prices by 10%.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: A 10% price cut shrinks the profit margin on every watch sold, yet the boutiques still have to pay 14 specialist sales staff and rent. [k] Takings are already down to $95,000 per boutique a month, so lowering prices could erode profit further unless sales volume rises sharply. [app] Lower margins reduce the cash available to ride out the slump and could force staff hour cuts. [an] Problem 2: Heavy discounting can damage the exclusive brand image that convinces customers to pay high prices. [k] Keeping prices unchanged protects that exclusive image, but cutting prices by 10% may teach buyers to wait for discounts rather than pay full price. [app] If the exclusive image weakens, takings may never recover to $130,000 a month even when the slump ends. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies that a price cut reduces profit margins per unit
Identifies that discounting damages an exclusive/premium brand image
application_max_2: References takings of $95,000 vs $130,000 or the 14 specialist sales staff
References the exclusive brand image / 10% discount
analysis_max_2: Explains the margin/volume trade-off and its effect on cash (staff cuts)
Explains how a weakened brand image undermines long-term takingsRecovery

questions.question_text: Do you think Marlowe & Grey Fine Watches should cut prices by 10%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: No: cutting prices by 10% would shrink margins on all watches and risk destroying the exclusive brand image. [k] Takings per boutique have fallen from $130,000 to $95,000, but a 10% discount would erode what profit remains and encourage buyers to delay purchases. [app] The VAT cut from 20% to 15% already lowers shelf prices by about 4% if passed on, which stimulates demand without the firm cutting its own prices. [an] Yes: a 10% cut could attract cautious buyers who feel they are getting value, especially during the 12 months the VAT cut lasts. [k] Takings of $95,000 a month per boutique show demand is weak; a well-advertised 10% discount could clear slow-moving stock and draw customers back into the 2 boutiques. [app] More sales at lower margin could raise total profit if enough extra customers are attracted, but it is uncertain whether a slump can be discounted away. [an] Overall, the partners should keep headline prices unchanged and pass on the VAT cut instead of cutting prices by a full 10%, because protecting the brand and margin matters most for luxury goods in a slump. [eval] This is justified by the collapse in takings from $130,000 to $95,000; discounting heavily rarely restores luxury demand, so a modest VAT-linked saving is the safer move. [eval]

Identifies the demand-stimulation argument in favour of a 10% price cut
application_max_2: References takings falling from $130,000 to $95,000 and the VAT cut from 20% to 15%
References the 2 boutiques, 12-month VAT window or footfall fall
analysis_max_2: Explains the VAT pass-on as a softer demand stimulus (roughly 4% shelf-price fall)
Explains the margin/volume/brand trade-off and its effect on profit
evaluation_max_2: Reaches a justified overall judgement (e.g. keep prices, pass on VAT saving)

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Harlan Building Materials Ltd is a private limited company in Country X supplying cement, sand and aggregates from 2 depots. It delivers to building firms, housing developers and public works contractors across the region. It employs 46 people and revenue was $6.8 million last year. In March the government announced a $250 million national road-building programme over 5 years.

Harlan has been invited to tender for a $4.5 million contract to supply cement to 3 road projects. Winning would require buying 2 new delivery trucks costing $380,000 each and hiring 12 more drivers, an investment of $760,000. The directors must decide whether to tender for the contract, or stay focused on their 140 regular small customers and avoid taking on debt.

questions.question_text: Define 'taxation'.
questions.model_answer: Taxation is the compulsory payment of money to the government by individuals and businesses, used to fund public spending and services. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies taxation as compulsory payments to the government
Identifies that taxes are used to fund public spending/services

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Harlan Building Materials Ltd of government spending on road-building.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Public spending creates direct orders for building materials, so Harlan can win lucrative contracts such as the $4.5 million tender for 3 road projects. [k] The $250 million programme over 5 years guarantees demand far beyond what small customers alone would provide. [app] Benefit 2: Better roads improve distribution across the region, making deliveries from Harlan's 2 depots faster and cheaper and opening access to new customers. [k] [app]

questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Buying 2 trucks at $380,000 each costs $760,000, a large sum for a firm with $6.8 million revenue that could strain cash or require borrowing. [k] If the $4.5 million contract is lost or delayed, the trucks and 12 more drivers would sit underused, raising average costs per delivery. [app] High fixed costs from trucks and wages must be covered even in quiet months, so profit could fall sharply. [an] Problem 2: Relying on one big government programme makes the firm vulnerable if budget cuts or delays reduce the road-building. [k] The programme runs over 5 years, and public spending can change with a new budget or a downturn in the business cycle. [app] If the contract ends, Harlan would still have the trucks and drivers to pay, and selling trucks is hard in a weak market. [an]

questions.question_text: Do you think Harlan Building Materials Ltd should tender for the $4.5 million contract? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Yes: winning the contract would transform Harlan's scale and profitability. [k] Revenue is $6.8 million, so $4.5 million of work over 5 years is roughly two-thirds of a year's sales added steadily, backed by the $250 million national programme. [app] Spending $760,000 on 2 trucks and 12 drivers lets Harlan capture this growth and build a reputation for large public projects. [an] However, the investment is large relative to the business and depends on government spending continuing. [k] If the tender fails or the programme is delayed, the $760,000 spent on trucks would strain cash and leave extra drivers idle, while the 140 regular small customers could feel neglected. [app] Staying focused on small customers avoids this risk but means forgoing the fastest-growing source of revenue available. [an] Overall, Harlan should tender, but negotiate milestone payments and stage the truck purchases so cash flow is protected if work is delayed. [eval] This is justified by the scale of the $250 million programme; the opportunity outweighs the risk, provided contract terms are secured before spending. [eval]

Identifies the risk of dependence on government spending / a failed tender

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Haver & Grey Electronics is a private limited company in Country X running 4 high-street shops selling TVs, laptops and washing machines. It has traded for 9 years and employs 52 staff. Revenue last year was $11.6 million, down from $12.9 million. The rise in tax was announced in the March budget.

To reduce a budget deficit, the government has raised income tax from 20% to 23% and VAT from 17.5% to 20%. The shops report fewer customers and average spend per transaction has fallen to $310 from $355. Footfall has been falling for 6 months. The directors must decide whether to cut prices by 5% to win sales back, or hold prices and wait for the government's promise of lower inflation.

questions.question_text: Identify two government economic objectives.
questions.model_answer: Two government economic objectives are: (1) economic growth; and (2) stable prices (low inflation). Other acceptable answers include full employment, balance of payments stability and redistribution of income. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Names any two government economic objectives (e.g. economic growth, full employment, stable prices, balance of payments, redistribution of income)
Accept equivalent wording, e.g. low unemployment or low prices/inflation

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Haver & Grey Electronics' revenue has fallen.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Higher income tax from 20% to 23% reduces households' disposable income, so they cut back on big-ticket items such as TVs and washing machines. [k] This is shown by average spend per transaction falling from $355 to $310. [app] Reason 2: VAT has risen from 17.5% to 20%, pushing up prices in the shops and discouraging purchases; revenue has fallen from $12.9 million to $11.6 million across the 4 shops. [k] [app]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies that higher income tax reduces disposable income and consumer spending
Identifies that higher VAT raises prices and reduces quantity demanded
application_max_2: References spend per transaction falling from $355 to $310 or the 20% to 23% income tax rise
References revenue falling from $12.9 million to $11.6 million or the 17.5% to 20% VAT rise / 4 shops

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of cutting prices by 5%.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: A 5% price cut reduces revenue per sale when spend per transaction has already fallen to $310, eroding retail margins. [k] On revenue of $11.6 million, a 5% cut removes about $580,000 of income unless volume rises sharply. [app] The fall is caused by higher taxes rather than high prices, so a price cut attacks the wrong problem and profit could fall below sustainable levels. [an] Problem 2: A price cut could start a price war; rivals may match the 5% cut, leaving all shops with lower margins and no extra market share. [k] With 4 shops and 52 staff to pay, Haver & Grey cannot absorb prolonged losses easily. [app] A price war risks damaging the shops' reputation and could force cost cuts that harm service and staff morale. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies that a price cut squeezes revenue/margins
Identifies the risk of a price war / rivals matching the cut
application_max_2: References $310 spend per transaction or $11.6 million revenue / the 5% cut
References the 4 shops and 52 staff or the wrong-diagnosis point (taxes, not prices)
analysis_max_2: Explains the arithmetic: a 5% cut on $11.6 million removes about $580,000 unless volume rises
Explains why a cut cannot fix a demand fall caused by taxation (wrong instrument)

questions.question_text: Do you think Haver & Grey Electronics should cut prices by 5%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: No: cutting prices by 5% would sacrifice margins without fixing the real problem, which is reduced disposable income caused by higher taxes. [k] Spend per transaction has already fallen from $355 to $310 and VAT is now 20%, so a 5% cut would lower revenue further when sales have dropped from $12.9 million to $11.6 million. [app] Holding prices preserves the cash needed to pay the 52 staff and keeps the shops stocked; targeted promotions on slow lines are safer than an across-the-board cut. [an] Yes: a 5% cut could pull cautious households back into the 4 shops and rebuild footfall while rivals hold prices. [k] If the government delivers its promise of lower inflation, spending power recovers, and a visible discount now could make Haver & Grey the value destination in town. [app] More transactions at slightly lower margins could stabilise total profit, and winning customers now builds loyalty for the recovery. [an] Overall, the directors should not cut prices across the board by 5%; they should use targeted discounts and promotions instead, protecting margins while tempting back customers. [eval] This is justified because the fall in sales is caused by higher taxes and lower spending power, not by price perception, so a blanket cut would sacrifice profit for uncertain gain. [eval]

Identifies the argument for a cut (stimulates demand, builds loyalty)

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Penny & Thread is a private limited company in Country X running 3 discount clothing stores in low-income areas. The stores sell own-brand clothing, school uniforms and household basics at very low prices for cash-strapped families. It employs 27 staff and revenue last year was $4.9 million.

As part of redistributing income, the government has increased weekly benefits for low-income families by $30 per child and cut the income tax rate for low-income households to 10%. Footfall in the stores has risen 12% in the past 3 months, and shelves are emptying faster. The directors must decide whether to open a fourth store in a deprived estate at a cost of $600,000, or refurbish the existing 3 stores at a cost of $250,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'redistribution of income'.
questions.model_answer: Redistribution of income is the transfer of income from higher-income groups to lower-income groups, for example through taxes and benefits, to make the distribution of income more equal. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies the transfer of income from richer to poorer groups
Identifies the mechanism (taxes and benefits) or the aim (greater equality)

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the government's redistribution of income on Penny & Thread.
questions.model_answer: Effect 1: Low-income households have more money to spend, so demand for discount clothing rises; footfall in the stores has risen 12% in the past 3 months. [k] [app] Effect 2: Higher benefits of $30 per child per week and an income tax rate of just 10% raise disposable income, increasing sales of own-brand clothing and school uniforms at low prices. [k] [app]

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of refurbishing the existing 3 stores instead of opening a fourth.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Refurbishment at $250,000 costs less than half of the $600,000 needed for a new store, so the firm avoids heavy borrowing and keeps a cash cushion. [k] With revenue of only $4.9 million, committing $600,000 to an untested estate is a big financial risk. [app] Lower capital spending means lower financial risk and a quicker return on the investment, protecting profit and the 27 jobs. [an] Advantage 2: Upgrading the existing 3 stores keeps proven locations and customer bases while adding space and better displays to handle the 12% footfall rise. [k] The stores already sell own-brand clothing and uniforms that low-income families depend on, so improvements will directly serve current customers. [app] Refurbishment raises capacity where demand is already proven, so sales can rise with far less risk than opening in an untested estate. [an]

Identifies that existing stores have proven demand/customers

[app] Staying small protects the 27 staff and the proven customer base, but shelves are already emptying faster and customers may switch to rivals. unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Meadowgate Grocers is a private limited company in Country X operating 5 neighbourhood supermarkets. Each store carries about 6,000 product lines and trades 7 days a week. It employs 88 staff and revenue was $16.4 million last year. Fresh food prices rose sharply this year and inflation reached 6%, above the government's target of stable prices at 2%. Suppliers are demanding higher prices for milk, bread and fresh produce.

The government is committed to restoring stable prices and has asked retailers not to raise prices excessively. Meadowgate's costs have risen 8%. The 6% figure would be the first across-the-board rise in 3 years. The directors must decide whether to raise shelf prices by 6% in line with inflation, or absorb the cost increase by cutting staff hours and promotions.

questions.model_answer: Stable prices means the general price level in the economy rises only slowly, i.e. inflation is low and predictable, so money keeps its value. [2]

[k] [app] Effect 2: Customers' purchasing power falls as prices rise, so shoppers become more price-sensitive and may switch to cheaper goods; with about 6,000 product lines to re-price, the workload and pressure on staff increase. [k] [app]

[app] Lower volumes would spread the 88 staff's wages over fewer sales, raising the average cost per transaction and squeezing profit. [an] Problem 2: Raising prices conflicts with the government's stable prices objective, and the government has asked retailers not to raise prices excessively; bad publicity could harm the brand. unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Larchmont Dairies is a private limited company in Country X producing butter and hard cheese. It buys milk from 38 local dairy farms and churns 6 days a week. It employs 96 workers at one creamery and sells mainly to supermarkets at home, and its main export is hard cheese. Last year it exported $2.1 million of cheese, double the $1.05 million exported the previous year.

The government wants to improve the balance of payments and is offering a 15% export grant for 3 years, and has imposed an 18% tariff on imported cheese. The directors must decide whether to build a second production line costing $2.8 million to expand exports, or focus on the domestic market, where the tariff on imports should lift their sales.

questions.question_text: Define 'balance of payments'.
questions.model_answer: The balance of payments is a record of a country's economic transactions with the rest of the world over a period of time, including exports and imports of goods and services. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies the balance of payments as a record of transactions with the rest of the world
Identifies that it includes exports and imports of goods and services

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Larchmont Dairies of exporting more cheese.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Export sales earn foreign currency for the country, directly supporting the government's balance of payments objective; Larchmont's exports rose to $2.1 million from $1.05 million. [k] [app] Benefit 2: Exporting spreads risk — selling abroad reduces reliance on the home market, so an economic downturn in Country X would not wipe out sales at the single creamery. [k] [app]

knowledge_max_2: Identifies that exports earn foreign currency/support the balance of payments
Identifies that exporting spreads risk/reduces dependence on the home market
application_max_2: References exports doubling from $1.05 million to $2.1 million

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of building a second production line costing $2.8 million.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The $2.8 million investment is large for one creamery employing 96 workers and may require borrowing, increasing financial risk. [k] If export demand disappoints, the new line may run below capacity, raising average costs and cutting profit. [app] High fixed costs would weigh on the firm even in quiet months, so the break-even point rises and profit becomes less secure. unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Coppermill Furniture Ltd is a private limited company in Redbrook, Country X, manufacturing oak dining tables and chairs. It employs 34 workers and recorded sales revenue of $2.6 million last year. In 2023 it borrowed $400,000 from its bank at 5% annual interest to buy machinery. Two years of repayments have been made and the outstanding balance is $300,000.

The central bank has raised its base rate from 5% to 9%, so the rate on the outstanding balance will rise to 9% next month, adding $12,000 a year to interest costs. Owner Priya Raman wants to open a second workshop costing $180,000, funded by a further loan at 10% costing about $18,000 a year in interest. The order book is full for the next 6 months, but Priya fears customers may spend less if rates stay high. She must decide whether to expand now or wait until rates fall.

questions.model_answer: One effect is higher interest payments on the outstanding loan, which reduce profit. A second effect is less cash available to fund other spending or expansion, which may force the business to delay plans. [2]
