More expensive expansion finance: the proposed second workshop would need a further loan at 10%, costing about $18,000 a year in interest [k], which may make the $180,000 expansion hard to justify if customers spend less while rates stay high [app].

As buyers postpone big-ticket purchases, Coppermill's order book may shorten from its current 6 months, cutting future revenue [an]. Attractive savings returns: higher rates make saving more rewarding, so households save rather than spend [k], meaning demand for non-essential items like oak furniture falls [app], which would leave Coppermill with unsold stock and lower cash inflow [an].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Halden Motors is an independent car dealership in Dunmore, Country X, selling new and used family cars. It employs 12 sales staff and 6 service technicians, and sold 210 cars last year with revenue of $4.3 million. Around 70% of buyers use finance packages arranged through the dealership, and the average new car costs about $19,000.

The central bank has cut its base interest rate from 6% to 3% to encourage spending. Weekly finance applications at Halden Motors have risen from 18 to 29, and rival dealers are expanding their forecourts. questions.question_text: Outline what is meant by the 'base rate' of interest.

Economies of bulk buying: ordering 40 cars at once may earn volume discounts from manufacturers [k], reducing the cost of each additional car [app], and with finance demand this strong the extra stock should sell quickly, protecting cash flow [an].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Eastmoor Budget Hotel is a private limited company in Millbrook, Country X, with 110 rooms near the Eastmoor industrial estate. It employs 42 staff and averages 55% occupancy, earning revenue of $2.4 million last year. In January the town's steel components factory closed with the loss of 900 jobs, pushing local unemployment from 3.5% to 7.2%. Inflation rose to 8% in the same period and consumer confidence fell sharply.

General manager Denise Whitaker has noticed business bookings are down 30%, while enquiries for weekly rates from job-seekers attending interviews have doubled. She must decide whether to cut the nightly room rate from $80 to $65 to stimulate demand, or introduce weekly rates of $400 for long-stay guests. questions.question_text: Outline two effects of rising local unemployment on a business.
questions.model_answer: One effect is that consumers have less income to spend, so demand for products falls. A second effect is that more workers are available to hire, making recruitment easier and possibly cheaper. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Higher unemployment reduces consumer incomes and demand
Higher unemployment increases the supply of labour available to businesses

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the factory closure has affected Eastmoor Budget Hotel.
questions.model_answer: Weaker demand from business travellers: the factory's closure with the loss of 900 jobs has cut local business activity and incomes [k], and Eastmoor has seen business bookings fall by 30% [app]. A new opportunity from long-stay guests: rising unemployment brings job-seekers needing affordable accommodation [k], shown by the doubling of enquiries for weekly rates [app].

knowledge_max_2: Higher unemployment reduces demand for business-related spending
Higher unemployment can increase demand for low-cost services from job-seekers
application_max_2: The steel components factory closed with the loss of 900 jobs and local unemployment rose from 3.5% to 7.2%
Business bookings are down 30% while enquiries for weekly rates have doubled

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Eastmoor of introducing weekly rates of $400 for long-stay guests.
questions.model_answer: More predictable occupancy: weekly rates give a guaranteed share of the 110 rooms each week [k], which suits the hotel's need for steady occupancy in the quiet summer months [app], improving cash flow and making staffing easier to plan [an]. Better use of empty rooms: at $400 a week the effective nightly rate is about $57, below the standard $80 rate but above a $65 cut applied to every room [k], so the hotel fills rooms that would otherwise stay empty [app], raising total revenue without discounting all rooms [an].

knowledge_max_2: Weekly rates provide predictable, guaranteed occupancy
Weekly rates can fill otherwise empty rooms without discounting all sales
application_max_2: Eastmoor averages 55% occupancy with 110 rooms to fill
Enquiries for weekly rates from job-seekers have doubled
analysis_max_2: Predictable occupancy improves cash flow and staffing plans
Filling rooms at an effective rate above the proposed cut protects revenue

questions.question_text: Do you think Denise Whitaker should cut the nightly room rate from $80 to $65? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Cutting the nightly rate could attract price-conscious leisure guests [k], and filling 15 extra rooms a night at $65 would add about $975 of nightly revenue compared with empty rooms [app], lifting occupancy above 55% and spreading fixed costs over more guests [an]. However, the cut would reduce revenue on the rooms that would have been sold anyway [k], while weekly rates of $400 match the doubled demand from long-stay job-seekers without cutting standard prices [app], leaving the hotel worse off if existing guests simply switch from $80 to $65 [an]. On balance, the hotel should introduce the $400 weekly rate rather than cut the nightly price [eval], because it targets the proven demand, with enquiries doubled, at less risk to standard revenue [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Cutting prices can stimulate demand and fill spare capacity
Cutting prices reduces revenue on sales that would have happened anyway
application_max_2: The nightly rate would fall from $80 to $65 with a possible gain of 15 extra rooms a night
Weekly rates of $400 match doubled enquiries from job-seekers

Existing guests switching to the cheaper rate would cut revenue with no extra occupancy
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation on the nightly rate cut
Judgement weighs extra occupancy against reduced revenue on existing sales

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Drayton Packaging Co is a private limited company in Country X, manufacturing corrugated boxes for food exporters. It operates 2 factories, employs 130 workers and recorded revenue of $6.8 million last year. Country X's economy grew by 3.8% last year, the fastest for a decade, helped by consumer spending and food exports rising 14%. Drayton's order book has grown 25% in 9 months.

Sales director Owen Pryce projects orders will rise another 20% over the next 12 months. Drayton can either recruit 30 permanent workers at a total wage cost of $900,000 a year, or meet demand through overtime at time-and-a-half and subcontracted production, costing an extra $250,000 a year. Overtime is already at 12 hours per worker per week, close to the legal limit, and two key customers want their supply contracts extended for 3 years.

questions.question_text: Define 'gross domestic product (GDP)'.
questions.model_answer: Gross domestic product (GDP) is the total value of all goods and services produced in a country in a year. It is used to measure the size and growth of an economy. [2]

knowledge_max_2: GDP is the total value of goods and services produced in a country
GDP is measured over a period, usually a year

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Drayton's sales have increased.
questions.model_answer: Economic growth: GDP grew by 3.8% last year, the fastest for a decade, so households and businesses spend more [k], lifting demand for packaged goods and therefore for corrugated boxes [app]. Strong exports: food exports have risen 14%, and Drayton's customers need boxes to ship produce abroad [k], which is why its order book has grown 25% in 9 months [app].

knowledge_max_2: Economic growth increases demand for goods and services
Rising exports increase demand for supporting domestic industries
application_max_2: Country X's economy grew by 3.8% last year, the fastest for a decade
Food exports have risen 14% and Drayton's order book has grown 25% in 9 months

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Drayton of recruiting 30 permanent workers.
questions.model_answer: Legal compliance and sustainable capacity: overtime is already at 12 hours per worker per week, close to the legal limit [k], so relying on overtime risks breaching regulations while demand may rise another 20% [app], making recruitment of 30 workers necessary to keep output lawful and safe [an]. Contract security: permanent staff would let Drayton extend supply for two key customers over 3 years [k], securing stable order volumes [app], and this stability supports revenue planning and investment in the 2 factories [an].

knowledge_max_2: Recruiting permanent staff raises sustainable capacity
Overtime is limited by law and cannot expand indefinitely
application_max_2: Overtime is already at 12 hours per worker per week, close to the legal limit
Two key customers want their supply contracts extended for 3 years
analysis_max_2: Recruitment avoids breaking legal overtime limits while meeting demand
Permanent capacity secures long-term contracts and stable revenue

questions.question_text: Do you think Drayton should recruit 30 permanent workers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Recruitment would let Drayton meet the projected 20% rise in orders next year [k], with 130 existing workers already on 12 hours overtime near legal limits [app], and would help secure two 3-year supply contracts, protecting a large share of $6.8 million revenue [an]. However, $900,000 a year in wages is a heavy permanent cost [k]; overtime and subcontracting cost an extra $250,000 a year and avoid long-term commitments if demand falls [app], so a downturn could leave 30 extra workers idle and profit fragile [an]. On balance, Drayton should recruit the 30 workers [eval], because the evidence of sustained growth (25% order growth, GDP at 3.8%) makes long-term capacity cheaper and safer than overtime [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Recruiting permanent staff meets rising demand with sustainable capacity
Recruitment adds permanent wage costs and risk if demand falls
application_max_2: Projected orders rise another 20% over the next 12 months with overtime near legal limits at 12 hours
Recruitment costs $900,000 a year versus $250,000 extra for overtime and subcontracting
analysis_max_2: Permanent staff secure capacity for 3-year contracts and revenue growth
If demand disappoints, 30 extra workers become an expensive burden
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation on recruiting the 30 workers
Judgement weighs sustained growth evidence against permanent wage risk

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Ainsworth Active Leisure operates 2 leisure centres in Country X, with a gym, swimming pool and fitness classes at each. It employs 64 staff and has 3,800 members paying an average of $42 per month, generating revenue of $2.7 million last year. Inflation is at 8.5% and interest rates are at 7%; Country X's consumer confidence index has fallen from 105 to 88. Some 620 members have cancelled or downgraded in 6 months.

Centre manager Lucy Hammond must decide how to respond. Option 1 is to cut standard membership from $42 to $35, which would reduce fee income by $26,600 a month before any new members join (3,800 x $7). Option 2 is to launch an off-peak membership at $25 for mornings only, aimed at retirees and job-seekers, without cutting standard prices. Renewals are due for 1,500 members next quarter.

questions.question_text: Define 'consumer confidence'.
questions.model_answer: Consumer confidence is how optimistic consumers feel about the economy and their own finances. Higher confidence encourages spending; low confidence makes consumers save instead of spend. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Consumer confidence is how optimistic consumers feel
High confidence encourages spending; low confidence encourages saving

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why gym membership at Ainsworth has fallen recently.
questions.model_answer: High inflation reduces real incomes: inflation of 8.5% means wages buy less, so consumers cut non-essential spending [k]; Ainsworth has lost 620 members in 6 months [app]. Low consumer confidence: the index has fallen from 105 to 88, so households feel pessimistic about their finances [k], and a $42 monthly leisure membership is an easy budget item to cancel [app].

knowledge_max_2: High inflation reduces consumers' purchasing power
Low consumer confidence reduces willingness to spend on non-essentials
application_max_2: Inflation is at 8.5% with interest rates at 7%
Some 620 members have cancelled or downgraded in 6 months

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Ainsworth of launching an off-peak membership at $25.
questions.model_answer: Fills quiet morning capacity: gyms are often under-used before noon [k], and an off-peak $25 membership could attract retirees and job-seekers looking for affordable exercise [app], turning empty capacity into extra revenue without cutting standard prices [an]. Protects standard fees: standard members keep paying $42, avoiding the $26,600 monthly loss a full cut would cause [k], while the off-peak tier widens the market to price-sensitive groups [app], building the membership base to offset the 620 cancellations [an].

knowledge_max_2: Off-peak pricing monetises spare capacity at quiet times
A separate tier avoids discounting existing customers
application_max_2: The off-peak membership at $25 targets mornings, retirees and job-seekers
A full cut would reduce fee income by $26,600 a month before any new members join
analysis_max_2: Quiet morning capacity becomes revenue without diluting standard prices
A wider membership base offsets cancellations and protects total income

questions.question_text: Do you think Lucy Hammond should cut standard membership from $42 to $35? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: A cut could win back some of the 620 cancelled or downgraded members [k], and at $35 Ainsworth might still keep more members paying something than losing $42 fees entirely [app], protecting footfall and class income across the 2 centres [an]. However, cutting the fee reduces income by $26,600 a month before any new members sign up [k], and an off-peak membership at $25 targets price-sensitive customers without discounting everyone [app], so a full cut may be unnecessarily deep while 1,500 renewals are due next quarter [an]. On balance, Ainsworth should launch the $25 off-peak membership rather than cut standard fees [eval], because the risk of losing $26,600 a month outweighs the uncertain gains from the cut [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Lowering price can stimulate demand and win back lapsed members
A price cut reduces revenue from existing members unless demand rises sharply
application_max_2: A cut from $42 to $35 would reduce fee income by $26,600 a month before any new members join
620 members have cancelled or downgraded; 1,500 renewals are due next quarter
analysis_max_2: Retaining price-sensitive customers protects footfall and ancillary income
The fixed monthly loss applies immediately while new sign-ups are uncertain
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation on the membership price cut
Judgement weighs certain monthly revenue loss against uncertain demand recovery

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Emmer & Oak Bakery is a family-run partnership in Country X, supplying fresh bread and rolls to 140 schools under a 12-month fixed-price contract worth $1.6 million. It employs 48 staff and delivered 2.1 million loaves last year. Since the contract was signed, inflation in Country X has reached 10%. Flour costs are up 35%, yeast and packaging up 18%, and oven energy bills up 25%.

Partner Mira Castellanos estimates the contract will lose the bakery $90,000 over its remaining 5 months if prices are not changed. She can either ask the schools' caterer to renegotiate the contract now, risking cancellation if the caterer switches to a rival bakery, or continue at the agreed price until the contract ends and then quote a higher price at renewal. The caterer has written a 3-month notice period into the contract.

questions.question_text: Outline what is meant by a 'fixed-price contract'.
questions.model_answer: A fixed-price contract is an agreement where the price stays the same for a set period, no matter how costs change. It gives the buyer price certainty but can hurt the supplier if costs rise. [2]

knowledge_max_2: A fixed-price contract keeps the price unchanged for a set period
Fixed-price contracts give the buyer certainty but shift cost risk onto the supplier

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Emmer & Oak's costs have increased.
questions.model_answer: Rising raw material costs: inflation of 10% has pushed flour prices up 35% and yeast and packaging up 18% [k], so every one of the 2.1 million loaves costs more to produce [app]. Higher energy bills: oven energy costs have risen 25% [k], which is significant for a bakery running ovens throughout the day [app].

knowledge_max_2: Inflation raises raw material costs
Inflation raises energy and utility costs
application_max_2: Flour costs are up 35% and yeast and packaging up 18%
Oven energy bills are up 25% for a bakery delivering 2.1 million loaves a year

questions.question_text: Explain two risks for Emmer & Oak of asking the caterer to renegotiate now.
questions.model_answer: Loss of the contract: if the caterer refuses and invokes the 3-month notice period, the bakery could lose a $1.6 million contract to a rival [k], cancelling roughly $133,000 of monthly revenue and putting 48 jobs at risk [app], leaving the ovens idle and fixed costs uncovered [an]. Damaged relationships: challenging a signed contract may make the caterer distrust future deals [k], and the schools' caterer may warn other public buyers about the bakery [app], making it harder to win the renewal or new contracts [an].

knowledge_max_2: A buyer may cancel a contract under the notice period if asked to renegotiate
Challenging a contract can damage the supplier-buyer relationship
application_max_2: The caterer has written a 3-month notice period into the contract
The contract is worth $1.6 million a year supplying 140 schools, with 48 staff dependent on it
analysis_max_2: Cancellation removes roughly $133,000 of monthly revenue and threatens jobs
Reputation damage reduces the chance of winning the renewal or future bids

questions.question_text: Do you think Mira Castellanos should ask the caterer to renegotiate the contract now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Renegotiating now could stop the bakery losing $90,000 over its remaining 5 months [k], and with flour up 35% and oven energy up 25%, continuing at the agreed price is unsustainable for 48 staff [app], so an honest conversation backed by cost evidence might be accepted by the caterer [an]. However, renegotiation risks cancellation under the 3-month notice period, losing $1.6 million a year [k], and the caterer could simply switch to a rival bakery rather than pay more mid-contract [app], leaving the bakery with idle ovens and wages it cannot cover [an]. On balance, Mira should wait until renewal and quote a higher price then, while absorbing a controlled loss now [eval], because protecting a 12-month customer relationship is worth more than $90,000 [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Renegotiating can recover rising costs on a fixed-price contract
Renegotiating risks cancellation and losing the customer
application_max_2: The contract will lose $90,000 over its remaining 5 months at current costs
The caterer has a 3-month notice period and could switch to a rival bakery
analysis_max_2: Successful renegotiation stops the $90,000 loss and stabilises margins
Cancellation removes $1.6 million of annual revenue and threatens jobs and capacity
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation on renegotiating now
Judgement weighs the certain $90,000 loss against the risk of losing the whole contract

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Bramcote Homes is a private limited company in Country X, building family houses on a 9-hectare site. It has completed Phases 1 and 2 — 60 houses — and employs 85 construction and office staff. Phase 2 sold out in 8 months at an average price of $240,000. The central bank has cut its base rate twice this year, from 6% to 4%, and mortgage approvals have risen 30%.

Director Farah Qureshi plans Phase 3 with 24 houses costing $4.8 million to build. The bank has offered a loan of $1.5 million at 5%, repayable over 10 years with interest of about $75,000 a year. Bramcote holds retained profit of $2.2 million. Farah must decide whether to start Phase 3 now, launching in the spring selling season, or wait 6 months until rates fall further and use more retained profit to shrink the loan. House prices rose 3% last year.

questions.question_text: Define 'mortgage'.
questions.model_answer: A mortgage is a long-term loan used to buy property, repaid with interest over many years. For most households it is their largest single debt. [2]

knowledge_max_2: A mortgage is a long-term loan used to buy property
A mortgage is repaid with interest over many years

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why demand for Bramcote Homes' new houses may rise when interest rates fall.
questions.model_answer: Cheaper mortgage repayments: cutting the base rate from 6% to 4% lowers monthly mortgage payments on a $240,000 average house [k], putting home ownership within reach of more buyers [app]. Higher mortgage approvals: approvals across Country X have risen 30% since the cut [k], showing that more households are being approved to borrow [app].

knowledge_max_2: Lower interest rates reduce mortgage repayments
Lower interest rates make banks more willing to lend
application_max_2: Bramcote sells houses at an average price of $240,000 on a 9-hectare site
Mortgage approvals have risen 30% after the cut from 6% to 4%

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Bramcote of borrowing $1.5 million at 5% to start Phase 3 now.
questions.model_answer: Starting now matches buyer demand: mortgage approvals have risen 30% and rates are at 4% [k], so launching 24 houses in the spring selling season after Phase 2 sold out in 8 months captures buyers at peak confidence [app], potentially generating revenue near $5.76 million (24 x $240,000) [an]. Retained profit stays available: the loan of $1.5 million at 5% costs about $75,000 a year in interest [k], leaving Bramcote's $2.2 million retained profit as a cushion for overheads and delays [app], which protects cash flow if any houses sell slowly [an].

knowledge_max_2: Starting at a peak-demand moment maximises sales
Borrowing preserves internal finance for other needs
application_max_2: Phase 2 sold out in 8 months and mortgage approvals have risen 30%
The loan of $1.5 million at 5% costs about $75,000 a year, leaving $2.2 million retained profit intact
analysis_max_2: Early launch captures peak demand and raises revenue
Preserving retained profit protects cash flow against delays

questions.question_text: Do you think Farah Qureshi should borrow $1.5 million at 5% to start Phase 3 now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Starting now could secure strong sales: mortgage approvals are up 30% and Phase 2 sold out in 8 months, so 24 houses launched in spring could sell quickly [k], revenue potential near $5.76 million against $75,000 a year interest [app], lifting profit and strengthening Bramcote's market position [an]. However, borrowing now means $75,000 a year interest for 10 years, and rates might fall further, making a larger retained-profit contribution cheaper later [k]; waiting 6 months could let Farah shrink the loan and reduce interest [app], but house prices rose 3% last year and competitors may launch first, eroding first-mover advantage [an]. On balance, Farah should start Phase 3 now with the loan [eval], because demand evidence (approvals up 30%) outweighs the modest risk of slightly higher interest [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Starting now exploits peak demand and first-mover advantage
Borrowing creates fixed interest costs that are worse if rates fall later
application_max_2: Mortgage approvals have risen 30% since the cut from 6% to 4%
$1.5 million loan at 5% costs about $75,000 a year over 10 years
analysis_max_2: Early launch maximises revenue and market position
Waiting could reduce interest costs but risks losing buyers to rivals
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation on borrowing to start Phase 3 now
Judgement weighs demand evidence against interest-rate uncertainty

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Clearbrook Logistics is a private limited company operating a distribution depot in Country X, employing 140 drivers, warehouse workers and office staff. It delivers 1,900 tonnes of goods a week for supermarket customers and recorded revenue of $5.2 million last year. Regional unemployment has fallen to 2.1%, the lowest on record, and Clearbrook has 25 unfilled driver vacancies despite advertising for 4 months.

Operations director Mr Ellison must decide how to respond. One option is to raise driver wages by 10%, adding $3,400 a year for each of its 96 drivers, a total of $326,400 a year. The other option is to launch an in-house training scheme costing $60,000 to recruit and licence 25 local people with no prior driving experience. Two rival firms have already raised wages by 8%.

questions.question_text: Identify two problems a very low unemployment rate can cause a business.
questions.model_answer: One problem is a shortage of available workers, making it hard to fill vacancies. A second problem is pressure to raise wages to attract and keep staff, increasing costs. [2]

knowledge_max_2: A shortage of available labour makes recruitment harder
Low unemployment creates upward pressure on wages

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Clearbrook is struggling to recruit drivers.
questions.model_answer: Few unemployed workers: regional unemployment has fallen to 2.1%, the lowest on record, so almost all qualified drivers already have jobs [k], which is why Clearbrook has 25 unfilled vacancies after 4 months of advertising [app]. Rivals are competing for the same workers: two rival firms have already raised wages by 8% [k], so Clearbrook's current pay is no longer competitive [app].

knowledge_max_2: A shortage of labour makes filling vacancies difficult
Rival firms may outbid a business for scarce workers
application_max_2: Regional unemployment has fallen to 2.1%, the lowest on record
25 driver vacancies remain unfilled after 4 months of advertising

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Clearbrook of launching the in-house training scheme costing $60,000.
questions.model_answer: Cheaper than a 10% wage rise: the scheme costs $60,000 once, versus $326,400 a year extra for a wage rise across all 96 drivers [k], freeing cash for other needs such as vehicle maintenance [app], so profit is protected while vacancies are filled [an]. Grows a committed workforce: training 25 local people with no prior driving experience builds loyalty [k], and they arrive without holding rival offers created by the 8% wage rises elsewhere [app], reducing the risk of trained drivers simply leaving for competitors [an].

knowledge_max_2: In-house training can be cheaper than a general wage increase
Training internally can build loyalty and reduce turnover
application_max_2: The scheme costs $60,000 versus $326,400 a year for a 10% wage rise across 96 drivers
It would recruit and licence 25 local people with no prior driving experience
analysis_max_2: Lower one-off cost protects profit and cash flow
Loyal new drivers reduce the risk of poaching by rivals

questions.question_text: Do you think Mr Ellison should raise driver wages by 10%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: A 10% rise would match or beat rivals who have raised wages by 8% [k], adding $3,400 a year per driver and costing $326,400 a year across 96 drivers [app], which should stop current drivers leaving and make the 25 vacancies easier to fill [an]. However, $326,400 a year is a permanent increase to fixed costs [k], while the $60,000 training scheme creates 25 locally recruited drivers who may stay loyal for years [app], and it could deliver capacity faster than hoping the tight labour market frees up qualified drivers [an]. On balance, Clearbrook should launch the training scheme rather than raise all wages by 10% [eval], because $60,000 versus $326,400 a year is strongly better value for filling the vacancies [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Raising wages helps attract and retain scarce labour
Raising wages permanently increases fixed costs
application_max_2: A 10% rise adds $3,400 a year per driver and $326,400 a year across 96 drivers
The alternative training scheme costs $60,000 once to licence 25 local people
analysis_max_2: Competitive wages stem turnover and fill vacancies
A permanent wage increase erodes profit if demand or margins weaken
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation on the 10% wage rise
Judgement weighs $326,400 a year against a one-off $60,000 training cost

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
PalmCrest Estates is a private limited company operating 11,000 hectares of palm oil plantations in Country X, established 9 years ago by founder Renata Duarte. It employs 520 plantation workers and exports $6,800,000 of crude palm oil annually. To double output, the company plans to clear 1,500 hectares of remaining forest, expecting an extra $3,200,000 in annual sales.

Environmental groups claim the forest holds endangered primates and have organised a petition signed by 45,000 people. The government now requires an environmental impact assessment before any clearing, with fines of $500,000 for illegal logging. The board is weighing this against an alternative: buy 800 hectares of degraded, already-cleared land for $2,100,000, suited to replanting but with lower yields for the first 6 years of cultivation.

questions.question_text: Define 'deforestation'.
questions.model_answer: The clearing and permanent removal of trees and forest cover from land, usually to make way for farming, logging or development [2].

knowledge_max_2: clearing and permanent removal of trees and forest cover
to make way for farming, logging or development

questions.question_text: Explain two problems that clearing 1,500 hectares of forest could cause for PalmCrest Estates.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Legal penalties [k], the government now requires an environmental impact assessment and illegal logging brings fines of $500,000 [app]. Problem 2: Reputational damage and lost sales [k], the petition signed by 45,000 people shows strong opposition to clearing the forest [app].

knowledge_max_2: legal penalties / fines
reputational damage / lost sales

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for PalmCrest Estates of buying the 800 hectares of degraded land instead of clearing the forest.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: No legal risk [k], already-cleared degraded land avoids the environmental impact assessment problem and the $500,000 illegal logging fine [app], removing the risk of losing the expansion programme [an]. Advantage 2: Protects reputation and exports [k], replanting degraded land keeps the $6,800,000 export business safe from the 45,000-signature petition [app], supporting continued sales growth [an].

knowledge_max_2: no legal risk / compliance
protects reputation and exports
analysis_max_2: removing the risk of losing the expansion programme
supporting continued sales growth

questions.question_text: Do you think PalmCrest Estates should buy the degraded land instead of clearing the 1,500 hectares of forest? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Buying the degraded land avoids fines and rejection [k], because the government requires an environmental impact assessment and illegal logging brings fines of $500,000 [app], protecting the company's legal position and expansion plan [an]. It also safeguards the $6,800,000 export business, since buyers increasingly prefer sustainable palm oil while 45,000 people have signed the petition [app], securing long-term contracts [an]. However, the price is well below the $1.80 domestic rate [k], so Redmire must check that higher volumes still cover costs and the four quality audits a year [app]; failing an audit could lose the 3-year deal after Redmire has committed $72,000 of its own money [an]. unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Wharfdale Cement Co is a private limited company in Country X, close to the northern quarry belt. It produced 180,000 tonnes of cement last year at a cost of $38 a tonne and sells at $52 a tonne, employing 64 workers. Domestic demand has grown slowly, at about 3% a year, and imports from Country Z have undercut its prices.

The directors are weighing two options: invest $2.4 million in a grinding plant in Country Y, where construction is booming and labour is 30% cheaper, or spend $1.1 million upgrading the Country X plant to export through the southern port. Country Y demand is projected at 400,000 tonnes a year, but the project needs a skilled expatriate team for the first 2 years and carries political and currency risks.

questions.question_text: Outline one benefit to a business of becoming a multinational company.
questions.model_answer: It can access larger markets abroad, increasing sales and spreading risk across countries rather than relying on one domestic economy [2].

knowledge_max_2: access to larger/more foreign markets
spreads risk / less dependence on the home economy

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Wharfdale Cement Co of building the Country Y plant.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: A Country Y plant would give Wharfdale access to a much bigger market [k], where projected demand is 400,000 tonnes a year, more than double its current 180,000 tonnes in Country X [app]. Benefit 2: Producing locally in Country Y would cut costs [k], because labour there is 30% cheaper, widening the $14 margin on each $52 tonne sold [app].

knowledge_max_2: access to larger foreign markets / more customers
lower operating costs from cheaper labour/inputs
application_max_2: 400,000 tonnes projected demand vs 180,000 tonnes produced now
labour 30% cheaper in Country Y; cost $38 vs price $52

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Wharfdale Cement Co could face if it builds the Country Y plant.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The overseas plant demands heavy capital [k], at $2.4 million versus just $1.1 million for the export-upgrade option [app], so cash is tied up for years and any fall in Country Y demand would sharply reduce returns [an]. Problem 2: Operating abroad brings unfamiliar risks [k], including the 2 years of expatriate management and the political risks the board foresees [app], which could disrupt production and make budgeting very difficult [an].

knowledge_max_2: very high capital cost / large upfront investment
unfamiliar country risks (political, currency, management)
application_max_2: $2.4 million for Country Y vs $1.1 million for export upgrade
2 years expatriate team; political and currency risks noted by the board
analysis_max_2: capital tied up; a fall in Country Y demand cuts returns
disruption risk and difficult budgeting in an unfamiliar country

questions.question_text: Do you think Wharfdale Cement Co should build the Country Y plant or upgrade the Country X plant for export? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Building in Country Y would let Wharfdale capture 400,000 tonnes of projected demand right at the customer [k], helped by 30% cheaper labour and the booming construction market [app], raising margins on each $52 tonne and spreading risk across two countries [an]. However, it costs $2.4 million, more than double the $1.1 million export upgrade [k], and needs 2 years of expatriate managers with political and currency risks [app], so a downturn in Country Y construction could leave an idle plant and stretched cash flow [an]. On balance, Wharfdale should upgrade the Country X plant and export through the southern port first [eval], because it is cheaper, reversible and tests overseas demand using existing strengths [eval].

knowledge_max_2: multinational location in growth markets brings scale and lower costs
overseas investment carries heavy capital and country risks
application_max_2: 400,000 tonnes projected demand; 30% cheaper labour; $52 per tonne
$2.4 million vs $1.1 million export option; 2 years expatriate team

evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation (export first vs Y plant)

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Dunharrow Woollen Mills is a private limited company in Country X that weaves woollen cloth for suit makers. It produces 60,000 metres a month, employs 110 weavers and exports 25% of output. Country X has removed most trade barriers on textile imports and signed tariff-cutting deals with 9 countries, and improved container shipping has cut delivery times to overseas buyers from 6 weeks to 10 days.

A tailoring group in Country Y has offered to buy 1.2 million metres a year if Dunharrow can weave to its specification within 12 months. Dunharrow could either export from Country X or discuss a joint venture to weave in Country Y. The owner, Marcus Whitfield, fears the Country Y partner may copy designs, but keeping all production at home limits how fast the order can be served.

questions.question_text: Define 'trade barrier'.
questions.model_answer: A government-imposed restriction on international trade, such as a tariff (tax on imports) or a quota (limit on the quantity of imports), used to protect domestic industry [2].

knowledge_max_2: a government-imposed restriction on international trade
examples include tariffs (import taxes) and quotas

questions.question_text: Explain two opportunities that the removal of trade barriers has created for Dunharrow Woollen Mills.
questions.model_answer: Opportunity 1: Lower trade barriers open larger export markets [k], and the Country Y tailoring group alone wants 1.2 million metres a year, far more than the 60,000 metres Dunharrow makes each month [app]. Opportunity 2: Faster, cheaper shipping widens Dunharrow's reach [k], because delivery times have fallen from 6 weeks to 10 days, making overseas orders practical [app].

knowledge_max_2: access to larger foreign markets after barriers removed
improved transport/communications make global trade faster and cheaper
application_max_2: 1.2 million metres a year wanted by Country Y vs 60,000 metres a month made
delivery times cut from 6 weeks to 10 days; deals with 9 countries

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Dunharrow Woollen Mills could face if it forms the joint venture with the Country Y partner.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Dunharrow risks losing its designs [k], because the Country Y partner would see its specification and could copy it once the 12 months are up [app], damaging Dunharrow's competitive advantage in woven cloth [an]. Problem 2: A joint venture splits control [k], so decisions about quality, output and price must be agreed with the partner [app], which can slow responses to faults and disappoint the tailoring group [an].

knowledge_max_2: risk of ideas/designs being copied by the partner
shared control slows decisions and creates friction
application_max_2: specification visible to partner; risk after the 12 months agreement
shared decisions on quality, output and price versus 1.2 million metres commitment
analysis_max_2: losing design secrecy destroys Dunharrow's competitive advantage

questions.question_text: Do you think Dunharrow Woollen Mills should serve the Country Y order by exporting from Country X or by forming the joint venture? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Exporting from Country X keeps Dunharrow in full control of its designs and quality [k], letting it earn the whole margin on 1.2 million metres a year through the 10-day container route [app], protecting the jobs of its 110 weavers and avoiding the risk of a partner copying its work [an]. Forming the joint venture would share the cost of weaving to specification and speed up the ramp-up within 12 months [k], giving local knowledge but splitting profits and ceding control of quality and price decisions [app], with the real danger of a future competitor armed with Dunharrow's specification [an]. On balance, Dunharrow should export from Country X [eval], because design protection and full margins outweigh shared setup costs, accepting a tight 12-month capacity challenge [eval].

knowledge_max_2: exporting keeps full control and captures full profit
joint ventures share cost/resources but split control and profits
application_max_2: 1.2 million metres a year; 10-day container route; 110 weavers; 25% exports

analysis_max_2: design secrecy and full margins vs partner copying and shared profits
capacity strain under 12-month deadline vs faster local ramp-up
evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation between exporting and the joint venture
weighs design protection/margin against speed and shared cost

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Stormont Electronics Ltd is a public limited company in Country X that assembles set-top boxes and routers. Its subsidiary in Country Z employs 480 workers and earned $6.2 million profit last year, of which $4.5 million was repatriated to Country X and $1.7 million was kept in Country Z as retained profit. The Country Z government has criticised foreign firms for moving profits home.

The board must decide whether to repatriate $5 million of this year's expected $6.8 million subsidiary profit to pay a special dividend in Country X, or reinvest it in a new assembly hall in Country Z costing $5.5 million. The Country X parent needs funds to upgrade its own factory, while the Country Z government hints that firms reinvesting locally may receive preferential tax treatment.

questions.question_text: Define 'repatriation of profits'.
questions.model_answer: The transfer of profits earned by a multinational's subsidiary or branch in a foreign country back to the parent company in its home country [2].

knowledge_max_2: profits earned abroad are returned to the home/parent company
typically by a multinational's subsidiary or branch

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages for Country Z of Stormont repatriating $5 million of subsidiary profits.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Country Z loses funds that could support local growth [k], because returning $5 million of the $6.8 million expected profit would leave only $1.8 million to reinvest or tax locally [app]. Problem 2: The host country gains less from foreign investment [k], so the planned assembly hall and its construction orders for local suppliers could be postponed [app].

knowledge_max_2: less money remains in the host country for reinvestment
fewer local benefits (jobs, supplier orders, taxes) from the MNC's presence
application_max_2: $5 million repatriated out of $6.8 million expected profit leaves $1.8 million
assembly hall ($5.5 million) postponed / local construction orders lost

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Stormont Electronics Ltd might choose to repatriate the profits to Country X.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Shareholders expect rewards from abroad [k], and paying a special dividend from repatriated profits boosts returns and may support the share price [app], which is why the board lists repatriation despite criticism from Country Z [an]. Reason 2: The parent company urgently needs funds at home [k], so repatriating $5 million could part-finance the Country X factory upgrade without new borrowing [app], improving productivity where head office and most owners are based [an].

knowledge_max_2: reward shareholders / pay dividends
fund home-country investment without borrowing
application_max_2: special dividend planned to be paid in Country X
$5 million earmarked toward the Country X factory upgrade
analysis_max_2: shareholder approval and share-price support despite host-country criticism

questions.question_text: Do you think Stormont Electronics Ltd should repatriate $5 million or reinvest it in the Country Z assembly hall? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Repatriating $5 million rewards shareholders and helps fund the Country X factory upgrade [k], continuing last year's pattern of sending $4.5 million home while keeping $1.7 million locally [app], though taking $5 million of the expected $6.8 million could worsen relations with the Country Z government and invite punitive taxes [an]. Reinvesting $5.5 million in the Country Z hall would secure the 480 workers' jobs, win the hinted preferential tax treatment and expand capacity near the market [k], but it leaves the Country X factory underfunded and Country X shareholders without their special dividend [app], tying scarce cash to one overseas site that faces political risk [an]. On balance, Stormont should reinvest in the assembly hall [eval], because the tax preference and host-country goodwill are worth more than this year's dividend, provided the board explains the decision clearly to shareholders [eval].

knowledge_max_2: repatriation rewards shareholders and funds the parent company
reinvestment secures host-country relations, jobs and possible tax benefits
application_max_2: $4.5 million sent home vs $1.7 million retained in Country Z last year
$5 million vs $5.5 million hall; $6.8 million expected profit; special dividend
analysis_max_2: risk of punitive taxes and worsened host-country relations from heavy repatriation
shareholder disappointment/underfunded home factory vs tax preference and job security
evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation (reinvest vs repatriate)

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Trevelyan Auto Parts Ltd is a private limited company in Country X making brake discs and hub assemblies for domestic vehicle assemblers. It employs 88 workers, sells 500,000 discs a year and had revenue of $9.6 million last year, growing at about 8% a year. A foreign multinational, Kestrel Mobility Group, is opening a vehicle assembly plant in Country X and wants Trevelyan to supply 700,000 discs annually under a 4-year deal.

To win the contract Trevelyan must install automated grinding equipment costing $800,000 and meet Kestrel's quality standard, which Kestrel's engineers would help install. unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Brentmoor Steel Plc is a public limited company in Country X producing steel rods and sheet for construction firms. It employs 320 workers, makes 90,000 tonnes a year at a cost of $540 a tonne and sells at $610. Cheap imported steel from Country Z, priced about 18% below Brentmoor's price, has cut its domestic market share from 30% to 22% in 2 years.

Country X's government is consulting on a 15% import tariff on foreign steel, which would raise import prices and shield local mills. Brentmoor's largest customers, two construction groups, oppose the tariff because it raises their building costs. The board must decide whether to lobby for the tariff or compete without protection by cutting its $540 cost per tonne.

questions.question_text: Define 'protectionism'.
questions.model_answer: Government policies that shield domestic industries from foreign competition, for example by imposing tariffs (import taxes) or quotas (limits on import quantities) [2].

knowledge_max_2: policies that shield domestic industries from imports
e.g. tariffs on imports or quotas

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for Brentmoor Steel Plc of Country X imposing the 15% import tariff.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: A tariff makes imported steel more expensive [k], narrowing the 18% price gap beneath Brentmoor's $610 and helping it win back market share from 22% [app]. Advantage 2: Protected demand would let Brentmoor use capacity fully [k], with its 90,000 tonnes a year and 320 workers better utilised rather than cutting shifts [app].

knowledge_max_2: imports become pricier; domestic goods more price-competitive
protected demand raises capacity utilisation and protects jobs
application_max_2: 18% price gap closed vs $610; market share fell to 22%

questions.question_text: Explain two disadvantages of the proposed tariff for Brentmoor Steel Plc's stakeholders.

Problem 2: Protection can reduce pressure to improve [k], so Brentmoor might delay cutting its $540 cost per tonne [app], leaving it weak if the tariff is later removed by trade deals [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Brentmoor Steel Plc should lobby for the tariff or compete without protection by cutting costs? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Lobbying for the 15% tariff would narrow the 18% import gap, lifting Brentmoor's $610 competitiveness and defending its 22% market share and 320 workers [k], but it risks alienating the two construction groups that buy much of its 90,000 tonnes a year and invites retaliation against Country X exporters [app], while discouraging the efficiency drive needed on the $540 cost [an]. Cutting costs to compete freely keeps customers loyal and prepares Brentmoor for any removal of protection [k], but trimming $540 per tonne below import prices 18% under $610 is hard and may mean wage or job cuts [app], with no guarantee of success [an]. On balance, Brentmoor should lobby for the tariff in the short term while committing to an internal efficiency programme [eval], because defending 320 jobs now matters and protection cannot be permanent [eval].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Marlowe Bicycles is a private limited company in Country X making steel-framed commuter bicycles. It employs 28 workers, sells 9,000 bicycles a year at $210 and has $1.9 million revenue. Two multinational retailers have entered Country X, selling imported bicycles at $150, and Marlowe's sales fell 20% last year while its market share dropped from 12% to 9%.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Drummond Chocolates Ltd is a private limited company in Country X making handmade truffles and bars. It buys cocoa from Country Y and sells 1.5 million bars a year at $3.50, employing 57 staff with $5.25 million revenue. A new free trade agreement between Country X and its neighbours has removed the 8% tariff on cocoa and on chocolate exports.

Drummond's board must decide whether to build a $1.8 million export factory to sell 2.6 million bars a year across the free trade region, or keep the single factory and rely on premium domestic sales, where it already holds 18% market share. questions.question_text: Explain two opportunities the free trade agreement creates for Drummond Chocolates Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Opportunity 1: Removing the 8% export tariff makes Drummond's bars cheaper in neighbouring countries [k], supporting sales of up to 2.6 million bars a year across the region [app]. Opportunity 2: Removing the 8% tariff on cocoa cuts Drummond's input costs [k], improving margins on every bar sold at home and in the region [app].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Suncrest Olive Estate is a private limited company in Country X producing gourmet olive oil for export. It sells 400,000 bottles a year at $9 each, earning $3.6 million, and 60% of sales (240,000 bottles) go to buyers in Country W. The Country X dollar has appreciated by 12% against the Country W currency, so Suncrest's bottles now cost Country W buyers the equivalent of $10.08 each unless it cuts prices.

Managing Director Lena Ortiz must set the June price list before orders for the next season close. Option A is to cut the Country W price to $8.10 a bottle, taking 10% off, to keep order volumes steady. Option B is to hold the $9 price and accept that Country W orders may fall sharply, shifting marketing towards domestic supermarkets instead.

questions.question_text: Outline what is meant by 'appreciation'.
questions.model_answer: Appreciation is a rise in the value of one currency compared with other currencies, so a currency buys more foreign currency than before [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the 12% appreciation on Suncrest Olive Estate.
questions.model_answer: First, appreciation makes Suncrest's oil more expensive for buyers abroad [k]. Each $9 bottle now costs Country W customers the equivalent of $10.08, so demand for the 240,000 bottles a year they buy may fall [app]. Second, appreciation weakens Suncrest's competitiveness against rival suppliers [k]. Country W supermarkets may switch to locally bottled olive oil instead, so Suncrest risks losing listings and part of its $3.6 million revenue [app].

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Suncrest Olive Estate might face if it chooses Option A.

At $8.10 instead of $9, Suncrest loses 90 cents on each of its 240,000 Country W bottles, which is $216,000 a year less export revenue [app]. If volumes do not rise enough to replace this, profit falls and less money is available to reinvest in groves and bottling lines [an]. Second, a lower export price can trigger a price war with Country W rivals [k]. Rival producers may match the $8.10 offer to keep their supermarket listings, so Suncrest gains little extra shelf space [app]. Margins then stay permanently lower across a market that takes 60% of sales, making the business less able to absorb future cost rises [an].

This keeps Suncrest competitive now that its bottles cost Country W buyers the equivalent of $10.08, helping to protect the 240,000-bottle order book that supplies 60% of its $3.6 million revenue [app]. Retaining shelf space prevents listings being lost to local Country W rivals, which would be hard and expensive to win back [an]. However, Option B holds the $9 price [k]. Refusing to discount protects the 90-cent margin on each bottle, so Suncrest avoids the $216,000 annual revenue loss built into Option A and keeps strong cash flow for the supermarkets [app]. The danger is that orders fall sharply as the 12% appreciation pushes Country W buyers towards cheaper local oil [an]. Overall, I think Suncrest should choose Option A [eval] because the appreciation was caused by currency markets rather than by Suncrest, and volume and shelf presence in Country W matter more than the margin; it can review the $8.10 price each season and raise it if the dollar weakens [eval].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Foxglove Denim Co is a private limited company in Country X weaving denim at its Glendale mill. It imports 30 tonnes of raw cotton a month from Country Z at $4,000 per tonne, costing $120,000 a month. The Country X dollar has depreciated by 15% against the Country Z currency, pushing the cotton price to $4,600 per tonne or $138,000 a month.

Managing Director Pavel Dvorak must decide on pricing by 1 August. Option A is to raise the wholesale price of jeans from $45 to $48 to protect profit margins, passing the $18,000 monthly increase to retailers. Option B is to keep prices at $45 and absorb the extra $216,000 a year, hoping cotton costs fall back or export sales to Country Z grow. 40% of Foxglove's jeans are exported.

questions.question_text: Outline what is meant by 'depreciation'.
questions.model_answer: Depreciation is a fall in the value of one currency compared with other currencies, so the currency buys less foreign currency than before [2].

Second, depreciation makes Foxglove's jeans cheaper for overseas buyers [k]. Lower retained profit means less money available for future investment, such as replacing weaving looms, which weakens competitiveness [an]. Second, Foxglove cannot know when cotton costs will fall back [k]. If the Country X dollar keeps depreciating beyond 15%, the $138,000 monthly cotton bill could rise further, so a fixed $45 price leaves the firm exposed to open-ended cost growth [app]. unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Ridgemont Electronics Ltd is a private limited company in Country X assembling smartphone accessories at its Darnwell factory, employing 85 workers on two production lines. It imports circuit boards from Country W, paying €90,000 a month under a rolling supply agreement. The exchange rate has moved from $1.30 per euro to $1.45 per euro, so the dollar now buys fewer euros than six months ago.

Finance Director Mark Delgado must decide before the October supply contract is signed. Option A is to switch to a Country X circuit board supplier charging $135,000 a month, invoiced in dollars, with a 12-month fixed price. Option B is to keep importing from Country W at the current $130,500 a month and hope the rate swings back, accepting the uncertainty.

questions.question_text: Calculate the dollar cost of the monthly €90,000 payment before and after the rate change.
questions.model_answer: Before: €90,000 x $1.30 = $117,000. After: €90,000 x $1.45 = $130,500. The depreciation raises the monthly cost by $13,500 [2].

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the exchange-rate movement on Ridgemont Electronics Ltd.
questions.model_answer: First, the depreciation of the dollar raises the cost of imported circuit boards [k]. The monthly bill has increased from $117,000 to $130,500, an extra $13,500 a month that Ridgemont must absorb or pass on to customers [app]. Second, the movement reduces the reliability of Ridgemont's cost planning [k]. If the rate moves beyond $1.45 per euro, the $130,500 monthly import cost rises further, so the firm cannot confidently fix prices in its October supply contract [app].

knowledge_max_2: A weaker dollar makes imports dearer
Rate uncertainty makes cost planning difficult
application_max_2: Reference to October supply contract / $130,500 vs $135,000

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Ridgemont Electronics Ltd might face if it chooses Option B.
questions.model_answer: First, the import cost is unpredictable month to month [k]. If the dollar weakens past $1.45 per euro, the €90,000 payment will exceed the current $130,500 and could approach the $135,000 charged by the Country X supplier [app]. Open-ended cost growth makes it hard to quote firm prices to customers, risking lost orders [an]. Second, continued importing keeps Ridgemont dependent on one foreign supplier and its lead times [k]. Any delay or disruption at the Country W factory would halt the Darnwell line that employs 85 workers [app]. A line stoppage would push up costs and damage reputation with accessory customers [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Ridgemont Electronics Ltd should switch to the Country X supplier (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A switches to a local supplier charging $135,000 a month with a 12-month fixed price in dollars [k]. For roughly $4,500 a month more than the current $130,500, Ridgemont buys certainty: its October supply contract can be priced firmly and its 85 Darnwell workers face no supply interruption [app]. Locking $135,000 removes the risk that the dollar weakens to $1.50 per euro, at which point €90,000 would cost $135,000 anyway [an]. However, Option B keeps the lower import price [k]. Overall, I think Ridgemont should choose Option A [eval] because fixed costs remove the guesswork from the October contract and a domestic supplier also shortens lead times; it can revisit the decision when the 12-month contract expires [eval].

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Carrowmore Cider Co is a private limited company in Country X's northern vale pressing craft cider from 300 tonnes of apples a year. questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the exchange-rate movement on Carrowmore Cider Co.
questions.model_answer: First, the appreciation cuts the dollar value of Carrowmore's euro export sales [k]. Second, the appreciation makes it harder to recover that revenue by raising the export price [k]. unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:

Founder Marta Kowal must choose how to buy next year's beans before the new season arrives. Option A is to sign a 12-month fixed-price contract at €2,800 a tonne with the Country W supplier, locking costs regardless of rate movements. Second, the cheaper euros give Thistledown more room to compete and invest [k]. Overpaying weakens the margin on every bag of beans and wastes funds that could finance growth [an]. Second, a 12-month fixed contract removes flexibility to switch suppliers [k]. unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Meadowlark Clothing is a private limited company running 9 clothing shops in Country X, trading for 8 years. It employs 120 staff and made revenue of $7.4 million last year selling mid-priced family fashion. Its own-brand dresses sell well, though Saturdays are the busiest days. All stock is designed in-house and bought from factories in Country X and Country Y.

A foreign online retailer, selling imported clothing 25% below Meadowlark's prices, now delivers to Country X in 3 days and advertises heavily on social media. Meadowlark's sales fell 12% last year and 2 of its 9 shops lost money. The directors are considering launching their own online store to sell across the region and halve delivery times, but building the website and delivery system would cost $400,000.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Velmont Electronics Plc is a multinational company assembling tablets and smartphones in 12 countries, trading for 26 years. In Country X it has proposed a $14 million factory to build tablets, employing 350 workers at wages 15% above the local minimum. It would pay corporation tax of about $2.2 million a year and use local component suppliers, but its profits would largely return to its home country.

Country X's industrial town of Brindleford lost its steel mill in 2019 and unemployment stands at 11%. The town council supports welcoming Velmont, offering a 10-year tax break worth $1.5 million, but residents fear traffic, noise and low-paid assembly work with little training. Local rival Darrow Components, employing 90 people, fears losing workers to Velmont's higher wages.

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Eastvale Bicycle Works is a private limited company assembling electric bicycles in Country X, founded 9 years ago. It employs 140 workers and produced 28,000 e-bikes last year, selling 70% abroad, with revenue of $11.2 million. Rising Country X wages and energy costs have pushed its production cost to $290 per bike, while rivals in Country Q make bikes for $230.

Country Q, a host country keen to attract foreign firms, offers Eastvale a 10-year tax holiday, wages one-third lower, and a $2 million grant. Moving would cut production cost by $60 per bike, but closing the Country X factory would make 140 workers redundant and Country X buyers would face about $9 extra per bike in shipping. The board must decide whether to relocate or stay at home.

[app] Reason 2: Host governments often offer financial incentives to attract foreign firms. [k] Country Q is offering a 10-year tax holiday and a $2 million grant for setting up there. [app]

[k] Shipping from Country Q would add about $9 per bike. [app] Some buyers may switch to rival brands, cutting Eastvale's home-market sales and damaging its reputation. [an]

[app] Lower costs would protect the 70% of output sold abroad on $11.2 million revenue and keep Eastvale ahead of rivals. [an] However, relocation carries heavy costs for stakeholders. [an] Overall, Eastvale should relocate only after exhausting home-efficiency options, since losing 140 workers and its domestic base is hard to reverse. [eval] On balance, the $1.68 million annual saving strongly favours moving in the long run, but the board must price in redundancy and transition costs before deciding. [eval]

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Northharbour Coffee Roasters is a private limited company in the port city of Northharbour, Country X, roasting coffee since 2011. It employs 32 staff and roasts 240 tonnes of beans a year, selling at $14 per kilogram to cafés and shops, generating about $3.36 million a year. Most beans are imported green from Country W.

In January the Country X government abolished the 15% import tariff on green coffee beans, fulfilling a free trade agreement with Country W. Northharbour's bean costs fell from $5.20 to $4.40 per kilogram, saving about $192,000 a year. However, the same deal lets Country W's larger roasters sell into Country X at only 8% above Northharbour's prices, and two Country W brands have already taken shelf space in Country X supermarkets. The directors must decide how to respond.

questions.question_text: Define 'trade barrier'.
questions.model_answer: A trade barrier is any government-imposed restriction on international trade, such as a tariff, quota or import licence, usually intended to protect domestic firms. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Government-imposed restriction on trade [1]
Examples: tariffs, quotas, import licences [1]

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the removal of trade barriers encourages globalisation.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Removing tariffs makes imported goods cheaper and more competitive. [k] Northharbour's bean costs fell from $5.20 to $4.40 per kilogram once the 15% tariff was abolished, saving about $192,000 a year. [app] Reason 2: Free trade agreements open markets to businesses from partner countries. [k] The Country X–Country W deal has let larger Country W roasters sell into Country X supermarkets. [app]

Free trade agreements open markets between partner countries [1]

Country W roasters now selling into Country X under the free trade agreement

questions.question_text: Explain two threats that the tariff removal creates for Northharbour Coffee Roasters.
questions.model_answer: Threat 1: Foreign competitors can now enter Northharbour's home market. [k] Country W's larger roasters can sell into Country X at only 8% above Northharbour's prices. [app] Their scale lets them undercut on supermarket shelves, threatening Northharbour's sales to cafés and shops. [an] Threat 2: Competition may force Northharbour to cut its prices. [k] Two Country W brands have already taken shelf space in Country X supermarkets. [app] If Northharbour matches lower prices, the $192,000 bean saving could be swallowed by a reduced margin on its $14 per kilogram coffee. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Foreign competitors can enter the home market after tariffs fall [1]
Greater rivalry puts downward pressure on price and margin [1]
application_max_2: Country W roasters can sell at only 8% above Northharbour's prices
Two Country W brands already taken shelf space in Country X supermarkets
analysis_max_2: Under-cutting at 8% or less erodes Northharbour's shelf position and café/shop sales
Price matching would absorb the $192,000 saving into a lower margin on $14 coffee

questions.question_text: Do you think the tariff removal will benefit Northharbour Coffee Roasters overall? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The tariff removal gives Northharbour a genuine cost advantage. [k] Bean costs fell from $5.20 to $4.40 per kilogram, saving about $192,000 a year across 240 tonnes. [app] Northharbour can hold prices steady, protect its 32 staff and reinvest the saving in quality and promotion. [an] However, the same agreement threatens Northharbour's home market. [k] Country W's larger roasters can now undercut within 8% of Northharbour's prices, and two Country W brands already occupy supermarket shelves. [app] If forced to match lower prices, the $192,000 saving could be wiped out, and Northharbour cannot match rivals' national advertising budgets. [an] Overall, Northharbour should use the saving to differentiate, such as launching speciality single-origin roasts that mass-market foreign brands cannot easily copy. [eval] On balance, the $192,000 annual saving is real but temporary, so long-term success depends on defending loyal café customers and a distinctive quality niche. [eval]

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity

Saltwick Shrimp Co is a private limited company fishing and shelling shrimp off the coast of Country X near the town of Port Saffron. Pelagia Seafood Group, a multinational company operating in 16 countries, has offered to build a $9 million processing plant in Port Saffron within 18 months. It would buy 600 tonnes of shrimp a year from Saltwick at $5.80 per kilogram and employ 220 local people, but wants Saltwick to stop supplying domestic processors. Its owners are abroad and say profits will be reinvested worldwide. The directors must decide whether to accept.

However, the 22% tariff would cut the margin on $40 million of sales [k], costing Varello roughly $8.8 million a year [app], so profits would be heavily squeezed every year the tariff remains [an]. Overall, Varello should build the mini-mill, because avoiding about $8.8 million a year of tariff costs soon recovers the $12 million investment and secures its Country X position [eval], while creating 150 local jobs would please the trade minister and reduce political risk [eval].

local production avoids the tariff and secures market access

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Veyr Cement Plc, a Turkish multinational, exports 200,000 tonnes of cement a year to Country X, generating $26 million in revenue. It has sold there for 5 years. Country X has introduced an import quota of 120,000 tonnes a year, starting in 3 months, to protect its national cement firms and cut dependence on imports.

Veyr's board must decide how to respond to the quota. It could build a $9 million cement plant in Country X, which would let it keep selling the full 200,000 tonnes, 80,000 of them produced locally, or reduce Country X sales to the 120,000-tonne quota and serve other markets instead. The new plant would employ 110 workers, and Country X's industry minister says the quota will last at least 4 years.

questions.question_text: Define 'import quota'.
questions.model_answer: A physical limit on the quantity of a product that may be imported into a country over a period of time [2].

knowledge_max_2: a limit on the quantity of a product that can be imported
set by government, often to protect domestic industry

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Veyr Cement Plc of building the Country X plant.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Veyr could keep its Country X volumes [k], producing 80,000 tonnes locally to top up the 120,000-tonne import quota and still sell the full 200,000 tonnes [app]. Benefit 2: Veyr would show its commitment to Country X [k], creating 110 local jobs, which may win government support and smoother approvals in future [app].

knowledge_max_2: local production bypasses the import quota volume limit
investment in local jobs builds goodwill with the host government
application_max_2: 80,000 tonnes produced locally plus 120,000-tonne quota = 200,000 tonnes
110 workers would be employed at the new plant

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Veyr Cement Plc could face if it builds the Country X plant.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The $9 million outlay is a big commitment [k], compared with simply redirecting sales to other markets instead of Country X [app], so if local production costs are higher than expected the investment could take many years to justify [an]. Problem 2: Veyr could become dependent on a rule-changing market [k], as the industry minister says the quota will last at least 4 years [app], so Veyr may face tougher restrictions later and struggle to leave the market once the plant is built [an].

knowledge_max_2: large upfront investment may not be justified if returns are weak
dependence on a market whose rules can change increases long-term risk
application_max_2: $9 million cost of the new Country X plant
industry minister says the quota will last at least 4 years
analysis_max_2: higher-than-expected local costs would make the investment hard to justify
once built, the plant makes Veyr vulnerable to further rule changes

questions.question_text: Do you think Veyr Cement Plc should build the Country X plant or reduce sales to the 120,000-tonne quota and serve other markets instead? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Building the plant would let Veyr keep selling 200,000 tonnes [k], holding on to $26 million of Country X revenue despite the 120,000-tonne quota [app], so turnover and market presence are protected [an]. However, the $9 million plant is a heavy outlay [k] and Country X could tighten its rules again after the current 4-year quota period [app], leaving Veyr exposed to a market it cannot leave easily [an]. Overall, Veyr should build the plant, because local production neutralises the quota and secures a key market for the long term [eval], while the 110 jobs created may improve relations with the ministry and ease future negotiations [eval].

knowledge_max_2: local production bypasses quota limits and protects revenue
large investments in rule-heavy markets carry dependency risk
application_max_2: 200,000 tonnes still sold with 80,000 produced locally vs 120,000-tonne quota
$9 million plant; quota to last at least 4 years; $26 million revenue
analysis_max_2: keeping full volumes protects turnover and market presence
dependency on Country X leaves Veyr exposed if rules tighten
evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation on building the plant
recognises the goodwill from 110 jobs may ease future ministry negotiations

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Zalvara Mining Plc is a Country X-based multinational that operates an open-cast bauxite mine in Country Z. The mine employs 850 workers and generated $300 million in exports last year. Country Z's government has introduced a new sustainable development law requiring foreign miners to restore mined land and cut carbon emissions by 30% within 5 years.

Zalvara's board must respond. It could spend $15 million on land restoration and cleaner haul trucks to comply, or relocate operations to Country Y, which has weaker environmental rules. The Country Z government has warned that foreign miners breaking the law face fines of $10 million and loss of their licence. Restoring the site would protect the mine for the next 15 years, but relocation would abandon $40 million of infrastructure already invested.

questions.question_text: Define 'sustainable development'.
questions.model_answer: Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs [2].

knowledge_max_2: meets the needs of the present generation
does not compromise the ability of future generations to meet their own needs

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Zalvara Mining Plc of complying with the new law.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Zalvara would keep its licence to operate [k], securing the mine for the next 15 years and avoiding a $10 million fine [app]. Benefit 2: Complying would protect Zalvara's reputation [k], as 850 workers and the local community would see it meeting the 30% emissions cut [app].

knowledge_max_2: compliance secures the licence to operate and avoids fines
compliance protects reputation with workers and the community
application_max_2: mine secured for the next 15 years; $10 million fine avoided

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Zalvara Mining Plc would face if it relocates to Country Y.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Relocation would strand huge past investment [k], abandoning $40 million of infrastructure at the Country Z mine [app], so Zalvara would lose capital that cannot be recovered [an]. Problem 2: Operating where environmental rules are weak is a short-term tactic [k], as Country Y has weaker environmental rules today [app], and if Country Y later adopts similar laws Zalvara faces the same compliance costs plus damage to its image as a responsible multinational [an].

knowledge_max_2: relocation strands capital already invested in the site
weak regulation is a temporary advantage as laws tighten globally
application_max_2: $40 million of infrastructure already invested would be abandoned
Country Y has weaker environmental rules
analysis_max_2: the lost $40 million cannot be recovered and would weigh on profit for years
future Country Y laws would impose the same costs plus reputational damage

questions.question_text: Do you think Zalvara Mining Plc should comply with the new law or relocate to Country Y? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Complying would secure the mine's future [k], keeping the licence for 15 years and avoiding $10 million fines after a $15 million investment [app], which protects a $300 million annual export operation [an]. However, relocating to Country Y avoids the 30% emissions cut and the $15 million outlay in the short run [k], though it abandons $40 million of installed infrastructure and relies on rules that may tighten later [app], damaging Zalvara's standing with governments and communities [an]. Overall, Zalvara should comply with the law, because keeping the mine operating over 15 years is worth far more than the $15 million cost [eval], and showing responsible practice may win it government support and community trust across Country Z [eval].

knowledge_max_2: compliance secures the licence and avoids fines but costs cash upfront
relocation defers compliance costs but strands assets and risks future regulation
application_max_2: licence for 15 years; $10 million fines; $15 million investment; $300 million exports
30% emissions cut avoided; $40 million infrastructure abandoned; weaker rules in Country Y

relocation loses $40 million of installed infrastructure and damages standing
evaluation_max_2: clear, justified recommendation on complying with the law
